answers.text: A worker may ride the forks for a very short lift when wearing a safety harness tied to the carriage.
A worker may ride on the load itself at low height because the forks are only just off the ground.
A worker may stand on a secured pallet on the forks to guide a load into a high rack by hand.
No person should ever ride on the forks, on the load, or on any part of the fixed telehandler outside the operator's seat, whether the machine is moving or stopped with a load raised.

questions.explanation: Forks and loads have no guarding or fall protection and can shift or drop without warning, so the only safe place on a telehandler is the belted operator's seat.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on checking engine and hydraulic fluid levels before operation?

answers.text: Engine oil, hydraulic oil, coolant, and fuel should be checked before operation and topped up only with the fluids the maker specifies for this fixed telehandler.
A low hydraulic level may be ignored for one load because the boom will still move, just a little more slowly.
Any oil on hand may be used to top up the hydraulics because all hydraulic oils work the same in a telehandler.
Fluid levels may be checked once a week because a fixed telehandler uses very little oil between services.

questions.explanation: Low or wrong fluids starve the boom, tilt, and steering circuits and can damage pumps before the first load is ever lifted.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on confirming boom position before looking up capacity?

answers.text: The operator first establishes the boom angle and extension that will be needed to place the load, then looks up the capacity for that position.
The operator looks up capacity after the boom is fully extended with the load already in the air.
The operator uses the most convenient boom position on the chart rather than the position the placement actually requires.
The operator looks up capacity for the position used to pick the load, even though placing it needs much more extension.

questions.explanation: Capacity changes as the boom moves, so the governing position is often the placing position, not the picking position. Checking that position in advance prevents discovering an overload mid-placement.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in warming the engine and hydraulics in cold weather?

answers.text: In cold weather the engine and hydraulic fluid should be warmed with a period of gentle operation before full loads are handled, because cold fluid flows poorly and cold parts are stressed by sudden full effort.
Cold weather has no effect on hydraulic performance, so warm up is wasted time on site.
Cold hydraulics respond best to immediate full speed cycling to warm the fluid by force.
A cold engine should be raced at high speed from the first start to reach working temperature quickly.

questions.explanation: Gentle warm up brings fluid and metal to working condition evenly, protecting seals, pumps, and the engine itself.

questions.question: Regarding travelling straight up or down a slope with a load, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: On a slope, the operator travels straight up or down with the load carried low and tilted back, keeping the heavy end of the fixed telehandler facing uphill as conditions require.
On a slope, the operator descends with the load facing downhill and raised high so the forks can be seen more easily.
On a slope, the operator turns the fixed telehandler around mid-grade with a load rather than backing to level ground first.
On a slope, the operator travels diagonally across the grade with a raised load to shorten the trip to the placement area.

questions.explanation: Side travel on a grade shifts weight toward the downhill tires. Going straight up or down with the load low keeps the machine far more stable.

questions.question: Regarding treating overhead lines as energized around the telehandler work area, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: The operator decides a line is a harmless communication cable by looking at it and works the boom close beneath it.
The operator treats an overhead line as dead because no sparks or sounds are coming from it while the telehandler works nearby.
The operator assumes a line with a dull covering is insulated well enough for the telescopic boom to brush against it.

The operator treats every overhead line as energized unless the utility owner has confirmed it is de-energized and grounded, and never relies on its covering or appearance to judge whether it is safe.

questions.explanation: Appearance cannot show whether a line carries power. Treating lines as energized until the utility confirms otherwise is the only reliable protection.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on maintaining visibility and using a spotter when the load blocks the view?

answers.text: When a bulky load on the forks blocks the forward view, the operator should travel slowly in the direction that gives a clear view or use a spotter to guide the fixed telehandler.
When the load blocks the view, the operator should rely on memory of the route because the yard layout rarely changes.
When the load blocks the view, the operator should raise the boom higher so the load clears the line of sight.
When the load blocks the view, the operator should lean far out of the cab while continuing to travel at normal speed.

questions.explanation: A load that hides the travel path hides people and obstacles too, so a clear view or a spotter must replace guessing before the machine moves.

questions.question: A telehandler crew is discussing cleaning up and reporting any fuel spill at refueling. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: A fuel spill may be covered with loose dirt and left, because soil naturally makes spilled fuel harmless.
Any fuel spill during refueling should be cleaned up promptly with proper absorbent material and reported as the site requires.
A fuel spill only needs reporting when it is large enough that the machine cannot be moved away from it.
A small fuel spill may be washed into the nearest drain with a hose so the parking area looks clean again.

questions.explanation: Prompt cleanup and reporting keep a small spill from becoming contaminated ground, a fire risk, or a hidden site violation.

questions.question: A telehandler crew is discussing highest capacities with boom raised and retracted. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: The highest chart capacities are found with the boom lowered and extended, keeping the load low to the ground.
The highest chart capacities are found with the boom raised and fully or nearly retracted, keeping the load close to the machine.
The highest chart capacities are found at mid-extension because the boom is balanced there.
The highest chart capacities are the same in every boom position, so position does not need to be considered.

questions.explanation: Keeping the load close in and high on the chart keeps its forward effect smallest. That combination is where the chart can approve its largest loads.

questions.question: Regarding auxiliary hydraulics powering approved attachments, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: Any attachment that physically connects to the carriage may be used, approved or not.
Auxiliary hydraulic lines may be connected under pressure to save time during a changeover.
Attachment weight does not count as part of the load because it stays with the machine.
Auxiliary hydraulic lines power approved attachments, and an attachment should only be used when it is approved for the machine and its weight is counted in the load being handled.

questions.explanation: Attachments add weight ahead of the carriage and change load moment, so approval and weight accounting keep the lift within capacity.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in carrying a load low and retracted to preserve stability?

answers.text: Traveling with the load carried low, tilted back slightly, and with the boom retracted keeps the combined center of gravity low and close, preserving stability.
Traveling with the load tilted fully forward lowers the center of gravity and prevents any spillage risk.
Traveling with the load raised high improves stability by keeping the forks clear of the ground.
Traveling with the boom fully extended balances the machine because weight is spread front to back.

questions.explanation: Low and retracted is the most stable travel position because it keeps weight near the machine and near the ground.

questions.question: Sam Rivera, a fixed telehandler operator working at a masonry supply yard, is working on checking entry and exit points for fit. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: At the site entrance, the operator checks gate width, overhead clearance, and turning room to confirm the fixed telehandler can enter and leave without striking posts, fences, or structures.
At the site entrance, the operator forces the fixed telehandler through a narrow gate by folding the mirrors and continuing even when the tires rub the posts.
At the site entrance, the operator judges clearance by eye from the cab and enters without checking the height of the raised cab or boom rest position.
At the site entrance, the operator enters through a pedestrian gate area because it is closer, without confirming the opening was meant for machine travel.

questions.explanation: Entrances set the limits for the whole job. Confirming fit before entering prevents the telehandler from becoming wedged or damaging structures on the way in or out.

questions.question: A telehandler crew is discussing tilting the carriage to keep the load settled on the forks. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: The carriage should be tilted fully forward while traveling so the operator can watch the fork tips at all times.
The carriage tilt should never be used at all, because the forks alone are meant to hold every load in place.
The carriage should be left tilted forward on a slope so the load slides off by itself at the landing point.
The carriage should be tilted back enough to settle the load against the backrest while traveling and tilted forward only when placing it.

questions.explanation: A slight back tilt cradles the load against the backrest, while a forward tilt invites it to slide off the forks.

questions.question: A telehandler crew is discussing leveling the frame before raising the boom on uneven ground. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Frame leveling is unnecessary if the load is light, because a light load cannot tip a tilted telehandler.
The boom should be raised first to check by eye whether the frame looks level enough for the lift.
The frame may be leveled after the boom is fully raised, using the raised load to help settle the chassis.
On uneven ground, the frame of the fixed telehandler should be leveled using the frame leveling control before the boom is raised or the load is lifted on the forks.

questions.explanation: Leveling first gives the boom a level base to rise from, so the load stays over the machine instead of leaning farther out as height increases.

questions.question: A palletised load for a fixed telehandler weighs 1,980 lb. The attachment used to carry it weighs 320 lb. The total weight the machine lifts is the load weight plus the attachment weight. What is the total lifted weight?

answers.text: 2,090 pounds in total
2,300 pounds in total
2,560 pounds in total
1,980 pounds in total

questions.explanation: Total lifted weight = load weight plus attachment weight: 1,980 + 320 = 2,300 pounds in total. That total is the figure the operator compares with the chart capacity for the actual boom position before lifting.

questions.question: A telehandler crew is discussing horn and backup alarm warning people around the machine. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Warning devices may be disconnected when their sound annoys workers near the machine.
The horn should be used instead of watching for pedestrians, since they will move when they hear it.
The horn and, where fitted, the travel or backup alarm warn people nearby that the machine is moving, and a machine with a failed warning device should have the fault reported promptly.
A failed backup alarm may be ignored because alarms are only fitted for parking lots.

questions.explanation: People on foot cannot judge a telehandler blind spots, so audible warnings are a working part of keeping them clear.

questions.question: Sarah Osei, a fixed telehandler operator working at a warehouse extension job, is working on using a spotter when the view of the route is blocked. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: When the view is blocked, the operator raises the load higher for a clearer view and travels without a spotter as a result.
When the view is blocked, the operator follows the spotter duties of sounding the horn continuously while driving forward blind.
When a load or site condition blocks the view of the route, the operator uses a trained spotter to guide the fixed telehandler and does not travel blind into the obstructed area.
When the view is blocked, the operator leans out of the cab and travels slowly, expecting pedestrians to move aside when they hear the machine.

questions.explanation: A blocked view hides exactly the people most at risk. A spotter becomes the operator eyes for the hidden area and can stop the machine before contact.

questions.question: Maya Singh, a fixed telehandler operator working at a precast yard, is working on setting both stabilizers before lifting a load that requires them. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Stabilizers may be set after the load is raised, once the operator sees how the machine settles with the weight.
Both stabilizers should be set firmly before lifting whenever the work requires them, rather than relying on the tires alone.
Only the stabilizer on the load side needs to be set, because that side carries most of the weight during the lift.
Stabilizers are optional on firm ground, even when the lift is planned at long reach with a heavy load.

questions.explanation: Stabilizers widen and steady the base before weight is taken, and setting them after the lift starts defeats their purpose.

questions.question: Aisha Bello, a fixed telehandler operator working at a hospital addition site, is working on longer load center reducing rated capacity. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: A longer load center only matters for loads that are also taller than the carriage.
A load whose center of gravity sits farther out than the chart load center reduces the allowable capacity, even if the load weight itself has not changed.
A longer load center increases allowable capacity because the load is better spread along the forks.
A longer load center has no effect as long as the total load weight is below the headline rating.

questions.explanation: Weight farther from the fork face has a greater forward effect on the machine. The farther out the center sits, the less weight the machine may carry there.

nccco-telehandler-rotating.quiz_title: CCO Telehandler Operator - Rotating Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on briefing crew on line location in swing arc?

answers.text: Only the operator is told about line location because only the operator controls the slew motion.
The crew is briefed once at project start even after the machine is moved to a new setup position.
The whole crew is briefed on where power lines sit in the swing arc and which slew sectors are restricted.
The crew learns line locations by watching where the operator chooses not to rotate the boom.

questions.explanation: Ground crew guide loads and walk the slew path, so shared knowledge of restricted sectors keeps everyone out of the danger arc.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in combined movement in wind?

answers.text: Keep combining movements in gusts if the tag line handler can hold the load.
Raise and extend the boom while slewing to present less area to the wind.
Use a quick combined move to beat a gust that is already pushing the load.
Avoid combined boom and slew movements in gusty wind, and slew with the boom steady until conditions ease.

questions.explanation: Wind acts differently as boom angle and slew direction change together, making combined moves unpredictable in gusty conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on avoiding sudden slew reversal?

answers.text: Avoid reversing slew direction suddenly, and let the load settle before rotating the other way.
Use rapid left-right slew inputs to damp out load swing quickly.
Reverse the slew at full speed to correct an overshoot past the target sector.
Reverse direction while the load is still swinging outward from the first turn.

questions.explanation: A sudden reversal doubles load swing and shocks the slew drive, so the load must settle before rotation changes direction.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in side sector capacity reading?

answers.text: Use rear values over the side because both sectors are away from the front of the machine.
Use the average of front and side values for a path that spends time in both sectors.
Use the over-side values whenever any part of the slew path crosses the side sector with the load.
Use front values for a side crossing that is brief, as long as the load ends over the front again.

questions.explanation: Even a brief side crossing is governed by side capacity, so the whole path must be checked against that lower value.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on boom elevation and gravity orbit?

answers.text: Extending the boom has no effect on the orbit if the load weight is unchanged.
Lowering the boom widens the gravity orbit more than raising it does.
Raising or extending the boom moves the load farther from the slew axis and widens the orbit of the combined centre of gravity.
Raising the boom pulls the load closer to the slew axis at every radius.

questions.explanation: Radius, not weight alone, sets overturning moment. A longer, higher boom places the same load farther out, so its orbiting effect on stability grows.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in pausing rotation in poor visibility?

answers.text: Rotation continues at night with site lights aimed only at the pick point and not the landing zone.
Rotation pauses when fog, dust, or darkness hides the load path, signaller, or tail swing area from view.
Rotation continues in fog using the signaller voice alone even when the load itself is invisible.
Rotation continues in dust because the planned slew arc was checked earlier in clear conditions.

questions.explanation: Slewing without seeing the full path removes every visual safeguard, so pausing until visibility returns restores safe control.

questions.question: Regarding leveling the rotating upper on outriggers, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: The operator levels the machine on its outriggers before slewing so the upper rotates on a true plane and charts remain valid.
The operator trusts the cab to feel level enough and skips checking the level indicator entirely.
The operator levels only side to side and ignores fore and aft tilt before starting to rotate.
The operator slews on a noticeable slope and compensates by rotating more slowly than usual.

questions.explanation: A level base keeps slew motion predictable and load chart values honest, while tilt adds side pull that grows as the boom rotates.

questions.question: A rotating telehandler crew is discussing parking with upper centred. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Park with the upper slewed to the side to save space in a crowded yard.
Centre the upper only when parking on a slope or for overnight storage.
Leave the boom raised at shutdown to keep the forks clear of the ground.
Park with the upper centred over the front and the boom lowered and retracted before shutdown.

questions.explanation: A centred, lowered upper is the most stable parked posture and keeps the boom and counterweight inside the machine footprint.

questions.question: Regarding control station changeover procedure, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: Change control stations only with functions neutral, the load landed or held, and the new station confirmed active.
Leave both stations active during changeover so either can stop the slew.
Assume the new station is active without testing a small slew input first.
Switch stations while a load hangs slewed over the side to save repositioning it.

questions.explanation: A controlled changeover prevents unintended slew inputs and confirms which station governs rotation before work resumes.

questions.question: A rotating telehandler crew is discussing slew motor leak check. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Check the slew motor and hydraulic lines for leaks that could reduce rotation control or holding power.
Check for slew motor leaks only after completing all planned lifts for the shift.
Top up hydraulic oil and ignore a steady leak at the slew motor for the rest of the day.
Wipe away slew motor leaks and continue rotating if the upper still moves in both directions.

questions.explanation: Leaks at the slew motor reduce holding and control pressure, so the fault must be reported and repaired before slewing with a load.

questions.question: Regarding rated capacity indicator sector display, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: Watch the rated capacity indicator as it updates the allowed capacity for the sector being entered.
Read the indicator only at the pick point because it cannot change while slewing.
Treat a falling indicator reading while slewing as a display fault rather than a sector change.
Assume the indicator display stays set to the front sector value through a full rotation.

questions.explanation: The indicator tracks boom position and sector, so its allowed value changes as the upperframe rotates with a load.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in hydraulic hose routing across slew joint?

answers.text: Chafing on hoses at the slew joint is cosmetic and never leads to failure.
Extra hose length at the slew joint should be coiled around the ring gear.
Hoses near the slew joint are routed and clamped to allow full rotation without chafing, stretching, or trapping.
Hoses near the slew joint should be pulled tight so they cannot move at all.

questions.explanation: Rotation works hoses back and forth at the joint every turn. Correct slack and clamping stop the rubbing and bending that eventually burst a line.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of barricading the tail swing radius, which of the following should a rotating telehandler operator affirm?

answers.text: The tail swing area is marked with a cone at one point and treated as blocked around the full circle.
The tail swing radius is barricaded or marked so no one walks into the path of the rotating counterweight.
The tail swing area is left open because workers are expected to notice the upper rotating toward them.
The tail swing area is barricaded only when the machine will slew beyond a half rotation.

questions.explanation: The counterweight sweeps a wide rear arc at body height, so a physical barrier protects people who may not hear or see it coming.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of travelling on slope with locked upper, which of the following should a rotating telehandler operator affirm?

answers.text: Descend slopes quickly to reduce the time spent in the tilted position.
Traverse slopes at an angle with a raised boom to keep the forks level.
Cross slopes slowly and directly with the upper locked and centred, avoiding turns on the slope itself.
Turn across a slope to shorten the route while the upper is locked and centred.

questions.explanation: Turning on a slope shifts weight sideways with no slew correction available, so slopes are crossed slowly, directly, and without turns.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of levelling after outrigger settlement, which of the following should a rotating telehandler operator affirm?

answers.text: Recheck level after the outriggers settle under the first load and correct it before further slewing.
Add packing under a settled jack while a load is suspended and slewed over it.
Correct settlement by slewing the load to the high side to balance the chassis.
Ignore slight settlement after the first lift and keep slewing for the rest of the day.

questions.explanation: Settlement changes the slew axis after work begins, so level must be rechecked once the pads have taken the initial loading.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of unlisted attachment has no capacity, which of the following should a rotating telehandler operator affirm?

answers.text: Use an unlisted attachment over the front only, where capacities are highest on the chart.
Estimate a capacity for an unlisted attachment by reducing the forks chart by a round amount.
Do not lift with an attachment that has no approved chart for this rotating telehandler model.
Borrow the chart of a similar attachment from a different model with the same boom length.

questions.explanation: Without an approved chart there is no rated capacity for that attachment in any sector, so the lift cannot proceed.

questions.question: Alex Morgan, a rotating telehandler operator working at a highway depot project, is working on rotation lock pin use. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: The rotation lock pin is left engaged to stiffen the machine on soft ground.
The rotation lock pin is engaged while lifting so the boom cannot slew at all.
The rotation lock pin is engaged for transport and when directed, to stop the upper structure turning on the chassis.
The rotation lock pin replaces the slew brake during normal lifting operations.

questions.explanation: The lock pin secures the upper structure for travel and transport only. Using the machine with it engaged would overload the pin and the slew drive.

questions.question: Sarah Osei, a rotating telehandler operator working at a hospital addition site, is working on marking the limits of the slew envelope. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: The operator marks the limits of the usable slew envelope on the ground so the crew can see where the upper may and may not rotate.
The operator marks slew limits after the first lift so the marks reflect where the load already traveled.
The operator marks only the pick point and leaves the rest of the slew envelope unmarked for the crew.
The operator keeps slew limits in mind only and expects the crew to guess where rotation must stop.

questions.explanation: Visible slew limits let everyone on site judge safe positions at a glance instead of relying on memory or guesswork during lifts.

questions.question: Kevin Doyle, a rotating telehandler operator working at a multi-storey framing site, is working on keeping load low during slew placement. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Raise the load to full boom height before slewing it a short distance sideways.
Carry the load high during slew placement to clear workers walking below it.
Keep the load just clear of obstacles and as low as practical while slewing it to its placement point.
Let the load rest on a structure midway and re-slew it onward from there.

questions.explanation: A low load lowers the centre of gravity and reduces swing energy during rotation, making slew placement steadier and safer.

questions.question: Marcus Webb, a rotating telehandler operator working at a school construction site, is working on retracted boom higher capacity. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Use retracted values over the front and extended values only at the final rear placement.
Use the higher capacities of a retracted boom only when the boom truly stays retracted through the slew.
Plan on retracted values and extend as needed during the slew to reach the placement point.
Keep retracted values if the extension is used briefly while crossing the side sector.

questions.explanation: Retracted values depend on the short radius they create; extending at any point moves the lift to a lower value.

nccco-rigger-level-i.quiz_title: CCO Rigger Level I Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on confirming load identity matches the rigging paperwork?

answers.text: The rigger rigs the nearest load without checking that it is the load described for the lift.
The rigger swaps the paperwork between loads so the closest load can be lifted first.
The rigger assumes two similar loads are interchangeable and rigs whichever is closer.
The rigger confirms the load in front of them matches the load described in the paperwork provided for the lift.

questions.explanation: Matching the physical load to its paperwork ensures the provided weight, balance, and attachment details actually belong to that load.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on why the hook must be over the balance point for a level lift?

answers.text: For a level lift, the hook should sit well to one side of the balance point.
For a level lift, the hook must be positioned over the load's balance point so the load hangs steady and even.
For a level lift, the hook should be over the lightest end of the load.
For a level lift, hook position does not matter because slings correct any tilt.

questions.explanation: A load hangs with its balance point directly below the hook, so offset placement makes it tilt and shift. Lining the hook over that point keeps the lift level.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in refusing to use questionable gear for one light lift?

answers.text: Light loads do not stress damaged gear, so inspection findings can wait.
A damaged shackle is fine for one light lift at the end of the day.
Using suspect gear once is acceptable if two people watch the lift.
Questionable gear must never be kept in use just because the next lift looks light.

questions.explanation: Damaged gear can fail well below its original rating, and no one can say where that new limit sits. A light load is still a load, so suspect gear stays out.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on adding sling length instead of flattening legs?

answers.text: When bridle legs would go flat, the rigger pulls the legs outward by hand during the lift.
When bridle legs would go flat, longer slings are used to raise the hook and keep the legs steeper.
When bridle legs would go flat, shorter slings are used to pull the hook closer to the load.
When bridle legs would go flat, the legs are crossed to gain steepness without longer slings.

questions.explanation: Longer legs raise the gathering point, steepen the pull, and reduce the extra stress that flat legs place on slings and hardware.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in using a hoist ring when the pull is angled?

answers.text: A hoist ring replaces an eyebolt when the pull is straight and no alignment is needed.
A hoist ring is used only for straight vertical pulls and locks against any angle.
A hoist ring is used when the pull will be angled, because it can pivot and align with the direction of pull.
A hoist ring should be jammed tight so it cannot swivel toward the pull.

questions.explanation: A hoist ring swivels and pivots to meet the pull, avoiding the bending that an angled load would place on a plain eyebolt.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in checking a provided attachment point for damage before rigging?

answers.text: The rigger connects rigging to a bent attachment point without mentioning it.
The rigger hammers a damaged attachment point back into shape and uses it.
The rigger covers damage on an attachment point with tape so it is not noticed.
The rigger looks over each provided attachment point for damage before connecting rigging to it.

questions.explanation: A damaged attachment point may not hold as intended, so checking it first and reporting damage prevents a failure during the lift.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in why synthetic web slings protect finished surfaces yet need edge care?

answers.text: A synthetic web sling is light and helps protect finished surfaces, but it is sensitive to cutting at edges.
A synthetic web sling is heavy and likely to scratch a finished surface by itself.
A synthetic web sling becomes cut resistant after it has been used for a while.
A synthetic web sling can be run over an unprotected sharp edge without concern.

questions.explanation: Flat webbing spreads pressure gently, which suits painted or machined parts. That same soft material cuts easily, so edges must be padded or avoided.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing checking metal mesh slings for broken welds. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Only broken welds near the handles of a metal mesh sling matter.
A broken weld on a metal mesh sling can be ignored if the mesh still lies flat.
A metal mesh sling with broken welds must be removed from service and not used to lift a load.
Broken welds on metal mesh can be re-welded in the field by the rigger.

questions.explanation: Welds hold the mesh fabric together and spread the load across it. Broken welds let the mesh pull apart and lose its grip and strength.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in never inspecting a sling by load testing it with a lift?

answers.text: Making a light test lift is the fastest way to prove a doubtful sling is safe.
A sling must never be checked by picking up a load with it to see if it holds.
If a sling holds a load once, any damage found earlier can be ignored.
A short trial lift is acceptable when there is no time for a full inspection.

questions.explanation: A doubtful sling can fail during the very lift meant to test it, dropping the load. Inspection is done by looking and feeling, never by lifting.

questions.question: Regarding confirming an eyebolt shoulder seats fully, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: The shoulder only needs to touch on one side for a light lift.
A shoulder that stands off the surface is fine if the threads feel tight.
A gap under the shoulder can be filled with a stack of loose washers.
A shouldered eyebolt must seat its shoulder firmly and fully against the load surface before lifting.

questions.explanation: Full shoulder contact lets the eyebolt bear load as designed. A gap invites bending at the shank and loosening under load, so the eyebolt must be reseated or replaced.

questions.question: Regarding setting a load back down and re-rigging when it tips or shifts, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: If the load tips or shifts on the trial lift, it is set back down and re-rigged before lifting again.
If a load tips slightly, the crew should push it level by hand while it hangs.
A tipped load should be landed at the destination and fixed after it arrives.
A shifting load can be corrected by moving faster so it settles in the air.

questions.explanation: A load that misbehaves inches off the ground will misbehave worse at height. Landing it and fixing the rigging is the safe correction.

questions.question: Regarding protecting a soft sling at the choke point, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: A soft sling is protected at the choke by twisting it extra times to spread the wear.
A soft sling can be choked hard on itself with no protection because the material is flexible.
A soft sling is never choked directly on itself without protection where the choke creates harsh rubbing or bending.
A soft sling only needs protection at the choke when the load has sharp corners elsewhere.

questions.explanation: The choke point is a high wear and stress area, so protection there helps prevent damage that could weaken the sling during the lift.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of rigging a load with provided keep-dry handling requirement, which of the following should a rigger affirm?

answers.text: The rigger rigs a keep-dry load while it sits in standing water.
The rigger removes protective wrapping from a keep-dry load before the lift begins.
The rigger leaves a keep-dry load uncovered in rain while waiting for the lift.
The rigger follows the provided keep-dry requirement and protects the load from wet conditions during rigging and travel.

questions.explanation: Moisture can ruin certain loads quickly, so honoring the keep-dry direction during rigging and travel preserves the load as intended.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing how a choker hitch changes a sling's usable capacity. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: A choker hitch keeps the full vertical rating in every situation.
A choker hitch grips the load by tightening around it, and it rates lower than a vertical hitch.
A choker hitch supports the load from underneath without wrapping around it.
A choker hitch rates higher than a vertical hitch because it grips so tightly.

questions.explanation: Choking adds bending and pressure where the sling passes through itself, which lowers usable capacity. The grip helps control the load, but the rating drops.

questions.question: Chris Dunn, a rigger working at a bridge construction site, is working on spotting bent links in a chain sling. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: A bent link found during the pre-use check means the chain sling must be set aside and not lifted with.
A bent link should be bent straight by the rigger and then used as normal.
A bent link is only a concern on the top leg of a multi-leg chain sling.
A bent link can be ignored if it still passes through the master link.

questions.explanation: Bending changes how a link carries load and can hide further harm. A sling with a bent link is not safe to use for lifting.

questions.question: Jordan Lee, a rigger working at a precast yard, is working on keeping a lifting beam level during the lift. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: A lifting beam is tilted during the lift to slide the load toward one side.
A lifting beam can hang tilted so one load point takes most of the weight on purpose.
A lifting beam is kept level during the lift so the load points below it share the support evenly.
A lifting beam level does not matter because its strength evens out any tilt.

questions.explanation: A level beam keeps the lower connections pulling evenly and stops the load from shifting toward the low side of the beam.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing using a tag line to control rotation rather than force a load. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: A tag line should be pulled hard sideways to drag the load into its final spot.
A tag line is used to control rotation and steady a load, not to pull the load into place by force.
A tag line can replace careful load placement by hauling the load the last few feet.
Handlers should lean their full weight on the line to swing the load over an obstacle.

questions.explanation: The line is a steadying aid only. Forcing a load sideways with it can overload the line, swing the load, and pull the handler off balance.

questions.question: Maya Singh, a rigger working at a power plant outage job, is working on communicating a rigging hazard clearly to the crane operator. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: The rigger communicates a rigging hazard clearly to the operator, describing what the hazard is and where it is located.
The rigger points vaguely toward a hazard and expects the operator to figure it out.
The rigger shouts a warning with no location when reporting a hazard to the operator.
The rigger tells a coworker about a hazard but never passes it to the operator.

questions.explanation: A clear description with a location lets the operator act on the hazard at once, instead of guessing while a load is ready to move.

questions.question: Jordan Lee, a rigger working at a commercial building site, is working on checking a shackle pin for worn or cross-threaded threads. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Worn pin threads are only a concern on screw pin shackles used outdoors.
A cross-threaded pin is acceptable if it can be forced the rest of the way in.
A pin with damaged threads can be swapped with any pin of similar size.
A shackle pin with worn, damaged, or cross-threaded threads must be removed from service.

questions.explanation: Damaged threads keep the pin from seating and holding properly under load. Forcing the pin makes the damage worse and hides a defect that can lead to failure.

questions.question: Priya Nair, a rigger working at a plant maintenance yard, is working on keeping hands clear while a load settles onto blocking. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Gloves make it safe to keep fingers in the gap during the final lowering.
A hand on the blocking helps guide it into final position as the load lands.
Hands stay clear of the gap between the load and its blocking until the load has fully settled onto it.
Holding blocking steady by hand is required until the load weight is fully on it.

questions.explanation: The closing gap can trap fingers in an instant as weight transfers. Blocking is positioned in advance and adjusted only when safe.

nccco-rigger-level-ii.quiz_title: CCO Rigger Level II Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in spreading the load when available lift points are weak or widely spaced?

answers.text: When individual points are weak, the rigger adds weight to test them before the real lift.
When individual points are weak, the rigger shortens the slings to increase their pull on each point.
When individual points are weak, the rigger concentrates the load on the one point that looks strongest.
When individual points are weak, the rigger spreads the load across more points or uses a spreader or lifting beam so no single point is overloaded.

questions.explanation: Sharing the load across points or a beam keeps each attachment within its limits, which protects both the load and the rigging.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in choosing the number of bridle legs for a wide load with four lugs?

answers.text: The rigger adds extra legs purely for looks and assumes each added leg automatically shares the load equally.
The rigger uses a single leg on a wide load and relies on a tag line alone to stop the load from tipping.
The rigger chooses the number of legs from the available pick points, load stability, and control needed rather than from habit or sling availability alone.
The rigger always uses two legs for speed even when four balanced lugs and a wide footprint call for a four-leg bridle.

questions.explanation: Leg count follows pick points and stability needs, so a wide load gets the control its footprint requires instead of the fastest rigging habit.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on sizing up a sling because a choker hitch reduces rated capacity?

answers.text: Size up to the next larger sling because the choker hitch rating on the tag is lower than the vertical rating and must still exceed the calculated load.
Ignore the choker rating and select the sling by its basket capacity, which is the highest number on the tag.
Use the vertical hitch rating to approve the choker hitch, even though choking reduces the sling capacity.
Use a smaller sling in a choker hitch because wrapping it tightly around the load adds extra strength.

questions.explanation: A choker hitch bends and compresses the sling, lowering its rating. Sizing from the choker rating on the tag, not the vertical rating, prevents an overload.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in why swing and snatch loading are dangerous to rigging capacity?

answers.text: Swing and snatch loading are dangerous because a swinging or suddenly caught load adds side forces and shock that the static rigging plan never accounted for.
Swing adds no real force if the slings are long, because long slings absorb all side movement harmlessly.
A snatch load is safer than a steady load because the brief duration means the sling barely feels it.
Swing only risks hitting nearby objects and never increases tension in the slings or hardware.

questions.explanation: Side pull and shock can overload a leg or pull a load out of its hitch, so the rigger prevents swing with control and tag lines where appropriate.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in re-checking connections after the trial lift?

answers.text: After the trial lift the rigger checks only the connections that looked loose from the ground.
After the trial lift the rigger sets the load down and re-checks every connection, pin, and shackle before the full lift proceeds.
After the trial lift the rigger skips re-checking if the load rose evenly the first time.
After the trial lift the rigger tightens connections while the load hangs at full height.

questions.explanation: The trial lift seats hardware under real load, and re-checking on the ground finds backed-out pins or shifted connections safely.

questions.question: Regarding predicting unequal sling leg shares from an off-center center of gravity, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: When the center of gravity is off-center, the unequal sharing disappears once the lift starts.
When the center of gravity is off-center, the legs farthest from it carry the largest share.
When the center of gravity is off-center, the sling legs nearest it carry a larger share of the load and must be sized for that unequal share.
When the center of gravity is off-center, every sling leg still carries an exactly equal share.

questions.explanation: Leg loads follow the center of gravity, so a rigger who assumes equal shares can silently overload the sling closest to the heavy side.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing communicating identified planning hazards to the entire lift crew. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Hazards found during planning, such as a shifting center of gravity or a tight clearance, are briefed to the operator, signal person, and rigging crew before the lift.
Only the crane operator needs to hear about hazards because the operator controls the load.
Hazards found during planning are kept with the lead rigger so the crew is not distracted.
Crew briefing on hazards can wait until after the load is set if nothing went wrong.

questions.explanation: A hazard only one rigger knows about cannot be avoided by the team, so the lift plan is briefed to everyone guiding the load.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on respecting temperature and chemical limits when choosing a synthetic sling for a plant pick?

answers.text: Chemical exposure matters only after visible damage appears, so no material check is needed during planning.
The rigger checks the working environment for heat and chemical exposure and chooses a sling material rated to tolerate those conditions.
The rigger uses the same synthetic sling near steam lines and chemical splash as in a clean warehouse because capacity is unchanged by exposure.
Heat limits apply only to the load itself, never to the sling that carries it through a hot area.

questions.explanation: Heat and chemicals degrade synthetic fibers, sometimes without obvious warning, so matching the material to the plant environment protects its rated strength.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of selecting beam and girder clamps matched to the flange profile, which of the following should a rigger affirm?

answers.text: Select beam clamps rated for vertical loading to take a strong diagonal pull from the side of the flange.
Select beam and girder clamps whose jaw design and rating match the flange profile and the calculated load when rigging from structural steel for a pick.
Select a girder clamp for a tapered flange using a parallel flange model because the screw pressure evens out the difference.
Select a beam clamp without checking its rating because the structural beam under it is far stronger than the load.

questions.explanation: Clamp jaws are shaped for specific flange profiles and vertical loading. A matched rated clamp seats fully, while a mismatched one can slip off the flange.

questions.question: Regarding checking eyebolt thread engagement before an equipment lift, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: Use an eyebolt with damaged threads after wire brushing them because the nut on top will compensate.
Use a longer eyebolt in a shallow hole and stack washers under the shoulder to take up the extra length.
Lift with an eyebolt threaded only partway in because a few full threads carry nearly the whole rating.
Confirm full thread engagement and a sound tapped hole before lifting, since an eyebolt develops its rating only when its shank is properly engaged in the load.

questions.explanation: Short engagement strips under load long before the bolt rating is reached. Full clean threads in a sound hole are what let the eyebolt carry its rating.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of coordinating travel speed with load stability, which of the following should a rigger affirm?

answers.text: The rigger keeps crane travel slow and steady for tall or wind-catching loads so inertia does not build into swing or tipping.
The rigger stops travel suddenly at the destination and lets the load swing to a rest.
The rigger lets travel speed stay constant regardless of load shape or height.
The rigger travels faster with a tall load so it spends less time in the air.

questions.explanation: Inertia grows with speed and load height, so slow steady travel keeps a top-heavy or bulky load stable and its swing manageable.

questions.question: Regarding checking the sling tag rating for the exact basket hitch planned, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: Assume the basket rating is always double the choker rating, so there is no need to read the tag for this hitch.
Verify the basket hitch rating on the sling tag against the calculated load before selecting it, because only that rating applies to the planned hitch.
Verify only the vertical rating on the tag, then use the sling in a basket hitch at twice that load without checking.
Select the sling without reading its tag because all hitches on the same sling share one common capacity.

questions.explanation: Each hitch has its own tag rating based on how the sling carries load. Checking the rating for the exact hitch planned is the selection step that prevents misuse.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing verifying a calculated weight against shipping papers and scale records. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: The rigger discards shipping papers whenever they disagree with a quick visual estimate.
The rigger trusts the lowest available weight figure so that smaller rigging can be used.
The rigger averages a calculated weight and a shipping weight without checking why they differ.
The rigger cross-checks a calculated weight against shipping papers or scale records and investigates any large difference before rigging the load.

questions.explanation: Cross-checking catches arithmetic and density errors, and a rigger should resolve a mismatch before the load leaves the ground on its slings.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing adding rigging and hardware weight into the total tension check for a heavy spreader assembly. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Rigging weight is ignored in the tension check because slings and bars are designed to carry themselves for free.
The tension check adds the weight of spreader bars, blocks, and the rigging itself to the load weight wherever that weight hangs below the hook.
Hardware weight is added only when it exceeds the load weight, which keeps the arithmetic simple for ordinary lifts.
Only the load weight counts at the hook, even when a heavy spreader assembly adds hundreds of pounds below it.

questions.explanation: Everything hanging below the hook pulls on the same slings and fittings, so heavy rigging weight belongs in the total the capacities are checked against.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing matching an electric chain hoist duty rating to repeated production lifts. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Select an electric hoist rated for occasional use to run continuous production cycles because the load is under its capacity.
Select an electric hoist by voltage alone and ignore both its duty rating and the calculated load for the shift.
Select the lightest electric hoist that barely covers the load for repeated lifts, since duty rating only matters for very heavy picks.
Select an electric chain hoist whose duty rating matches the planned cycle rate when the same calculated load will be lifted repeatedly through a shift.

questions.explanation: Capacity alone is not enough for repeated work. The duty rating must fit the cycle rate or heat and wear will shorten hoist life and risk a stall.

questions.question: A rigging crew is discussing how d over d bending affects wire rope sling capacity in substance. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: Bend diameter has no effect on wire rope as long as the rope does not show visible broken wires afterward.
Bending wire rope around a smaller diameter increases capacity because the tight bend locks the wires together.
Bending wire rope around a small diameter compared to the rope diameter reduces its efficiency and capacity because the wires are stressed unevenly around the tight bend.
Wire rope efficiency improves as the bend gets tighter, so the sharpest available edge gives the strongest lift.

questions.explanation: A generous bend lets the rope share load more evenly across its wires, so the rigger uses proper saddles and avoids tight bends that silently cut capacity.

questions.question: During a pre-work review of matching shackle bow size to sling eyes so nothing is pinched or side loaded, which of the following should a rigger affirm?

answers.text: Load the shackle from the side when the bow is too small, assuming the rating stays the same in any direction.
Select a shackle so small that the sling eye folds over the pin, because a tight fold prevents slipping.
Select a shackle with a bow large enough for the sling eyes to seat freely, so the load stays centered and nothing is pinched or side loaded.
Force two wide sling eyes onto a small shackle pin because pinching them together increases the connection strength.

questions.explanation: A cramped shackle pinches eyes and pulls the load off center. Proper bow size lets fittings seat naturally and keeps loading in the rated direction.

questions.question: Maya Singh, a rigger working at a shipyard staging area, is working on inspecting a load for hidden damage or weakness before deciding how to rig it. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: The rigger treats corrosion and rot as surface issues that never affect lifting strength.
The rigger skips inspection when a load was lifted successfully once before.
The rigger inspects for cracks, corrosion, rot, or prior damage that weakens the load and changes where and how rigging can be safely applied.
The rigger covers visible cracks with slings so they are supported and cannot be seen to worsen.

questions.explanation: Hidden weakness decides where a sling can bear, so a rigger inspects the load itself, not just the rigging, before the lift.

questions.question: Casey Thompson, a rigger working at a warehouse loading project, is working on sizing connecting links for the calculated tension not the sling color. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Select a lower grade connecting link for a high grade chain sling, assuming the chain will compensate for it.
Select the connecting link by its outside dimensions alone without comparing its rating to the leg tension.
Select connecting links that match the sling color because matching hardware is graded to work together automatically.
Select connecting links by rated capacity against the calculated leg tension, matching the grade of the sling they join.

questions.explanation: A connector of lower grade or rating limits the whole leg. Matching grade and exceeding calculated tension keeps the link from undercutting the sling.

questions.question: Jamie Carter, a rigger working at a steel erection site, is working on checking roundsling cover and core condition during a scheduled periodic inspection. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: A periodic inspection of a roundsling relies on stretching it by hand to judge the condition of its core.
A periodic inspection of a roundsling examines the protective cover for cuts and checks for damage or shifting in the load-bearing core yarns inside.
A periodic inspection passes a roundsling with a cut cover as long as no core yarn is completely severed.
A periodic inspection of a roundsling ends at the cover, because the core inside cannot deteriorate.

questions.explanation: The cover protects the core yarns that actually carry the load, so periodic inspection must confirm both are intact before the roundsling stays in service.

nccco-signalperson.quiz_title: CCO Signalperson Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in the hoist hand signal?

answers.text: For the hoist signal, the signalperson raises both arms overhead with the palms facing forward and holds them still.
For the hoist signal, the signalperson bends the arm, points the forefinger up with the forearm vertical, and moves the hand in a small horizontal circle.
For the hoist signal, the signalperson extends the arm downward, points the forefinger down, and moves the hand in a small horizontal circle.
For the hoist signal, the signalperson extends the arm sideways with the thumb pointing up and the fingers closed.

questions.explanation: A vertical forearm with the forefinger up, circled horizontally, is the standard hoist, so the circling motion cannot be confused with pointing signals.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on moving closer to overcome wind and background noise?

answers.text: When wind or noise garbles signals, the signalperson switches to unrelated words that carry better through the noise.
When wind or background noise garbles voice signals, the signalperson moves closer or repositions until the operator hears them clearly again.
When wind or noise garbles signals, the signalperson keeps transmitting from the same spot and hopes the operator guesses correctly.
When wind or noise garbles signals, the signalperson talks over the noise without checking whether any words were understood.

questions.explanation: Changing position against wind and noise attacks the barrier itself, restoring clear hearing instead of repeating a garbled signal.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on timing signals to work with a load's pendulum rhythm?

answers.text: To calm a swinging load, the signalperson signals random quick moves so the load cannot settle into a rhythm.
To calm a swinging load, the signalperson signals the operator to hoist rapidly, since height alone stops pendulum motion.
To calm a swinging load, the signalperson signals a hard swing in the opposite direction at the peak of each swing.
To calm a swinging load, the signalperson times follow-up swing signals to the load's natural back-and-forth rhythm instead of fighting the swing with opposing abrupt moves.

questions.explanation: Working with the rhythm settles a load faster than fighting it. Timed, measured signals let the signalperson shrink the swing with each pass.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on keeping the load path clear of people?

answers.text: Throughout the lift, the signalperson lets experienced crew members remain under a slow-moving load they are guiding by hand.
Throughout the lift, the signalperson watches the load path and stops movement if anyone enters the area the load will pass over or land in.
Throughout the lift, the signalperson clears the path once at the start and does not check it again during travel.
Throughout the lift, the signalperson warns people in the path by waving but keeps the load moving so the schedule holds.

questions.explanation: People drift back into work areas without noticing a load, so the signalperson keeps watching and stops rather than signaling around a person.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on understanding basic crane operation and its limitations?

answers.text: Understanding crane operation means the signalperson is qualified to make repairs to the crane when a limitation is discovered.
A qualified signalperson needs no understanding of crane limitations because the operator alone is responsible for every limit.
A qualified signalperson must have a basic understanding of crane operation and its limitations so their signals respect what the crane can and cannot do safely.
A qualified signalperson should signal for faster travel whenever a load is light, regardless of the crane limitations for that setup.

questions.explanation: Signals that ignore what the crane can safely do put the load at risk, so a basic grasp of operation and limitations shapes every signal given.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in flexing fingers duration in the raise boom and lower load signal?

answers.text: In the raise boom and lower load signal, the signalperson keeps flexing the fingers in and out for as long as the load should keep lowering.
In the raise boom and lower load signal, the signalperson flexes the fingers only after the boom has finished raising.
In the raise boom and lower load signal, the signalperson flexes the fingers faster whenever the boom should raise more quickly.
In the raise boom and lower load signal, the signalperson flexes the fingers once to start the load lowering and then holds them closed.

questions.explanation: The flexing fingers are the load-movement part of the combined signal, so continuing the flex tells the operator the lowering should continue.

questions.question: Regarding keeping constant communication and understanding, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: The signalperson maintains constant communication and understanding with the operator for the entire time the load is being handled.
The signalperson maintains constant communication and understanding with the operator by letting another worker take over without telling the cab.
The signalperson maintains constant communication and understanding with the operator only during the first lift of the shift.
The signalperson maintains constant communication and understanding with the operator by assuming silence from the cab means agreement.

questions.explanation: Continuous understanding means both parties share the same plan at every moment, not just at the start of the pick.

questions.question: Regarding positioning the device for hands-free speaking, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: The signalperson leaves the device on the ground nearby, because shouting toward it carries signals as clearly as speaking into it.
The signalperson holds the device in one hand throughout the lift, even when that hand is needed to stay balanced or safe.
The signalperson positions the communication device so they can speak and listen while keeping their hands free and attention on the load.
The signalperson lets the device dangle where its controls can be pressed accidentally during a transmission.

questions.explanation: A secure hands-free position keeps the signalperson focused on the load and their own footing while still sending clear signals.

questions.question: Regarding long loads and tag lines for a signalperson, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: When signaling a long load such as a beam or a pipe bundle, the signalperson expects the operator to spin the load deliberately to line it up.
When signaling a long load such as a beam or a pipe bundle, the signalperson expects the load to balance itself and needs no control of rotation.
When signaling a long load such as a beam or a pipe bundle, the signalperson expects handlers to hold the load directly with their hands at head height.
When signaling a long load such as a beam or a pipe bundle, the signalperson expects tag lines to be used so handlers can keep the load from rotating while it travels.

questions.explanation: Long loads act like weather vanes once airborne, and tag lines give the crew the gentle rotational control that crane signals alone cannot provide.

questions.question: A signaling crew is discussing obeying an emergency stop from anyone. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: The signalperson treats an emergency stop given by anyone on site as binding and stops all movement at once, regardless of who gave it or whether the reason is immediately clear.
The signalperson weighs an emergency stop from a bystander against the lift plan and continues if the load looks stable.
The signalperson accepts emergency stops only from the designated signalperson and the operator, ignoring all others.
The signalperson finishes the current movement before honoring an emergency stop so the load ends in a tidy position.

questions.explanation: An emergency stop may come from the only person who can see the danger, so the signalperson honors it first and asks questions with the load still.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in planning the load path to keep loads away from workers?

answers.text: Confirming the landing zone is clear is the receiving crew job alone, so the signalperson need not check it before signaling.
The signalperson should choose the shortest load path even when it crosses over an occupied work area.
Load path planning is unnecessary because the signalperson can redirect people out of the way while the load is already moving.
Before signaling a lift, the signalperson helps plan a load path that avoids occupied work areas and confirms the path and landing zone are clear of people.

questions.explanation: A path chosen and checked before the pick keeps the load away from people from the start, instead of relying on last-second warnings while the load is moving.

questions.question: Regarding signalperson repositioning during a long swing, which of the following statements is accurate?

answers.text: During a long swing, the signalperson hands the swing signal off to whichever crew member is closest to the operator.
During a long swing, the signalperson moves as needed to stay visible to the operator while keeping the pointing signal directed at the intended path.
During a long swing, the signalperson stays in the original spot even after the boom blocks the operator view of the signals.
During a long swing, the signalperson walks under the suspended load to remain in front of the operator at all times.

questions.explanation: Visibility is part of delivering a swing signal, so the signalperson adjusts position to stay seen while never letting the load pass overhead.

questions.question: Chris Dunn, a signalperson working at a bridge construction site, is working on the one-hand telescope in signal. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: When one hand must remain free, the signalperson signals telescope in by extending one arm sideways and waving the hand inward repeatedly.
When one hand must remain free, the signalperson signals telescope in with a single fist held in front of the body and the thumb pointing inward toward the center.
When one hand must remain free, the signalperson signals telescope in by holding one open palm facing down and pressing it downward.
When one hand must remain free, the signalperson signals telescope in by clenching one fist at the shoulder and nodding toward the cab.

questions.explanation: A single inward-pointing thumb preserves the retraction meaning of the two-hand form while freeing the other hand for balance or support.

questions.question: A signaling crew is discussing speaking clearly at a pace the operator can act on. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: The signalperson speaks clearly and steadily at a pace that leaves the operator time to hear, understand, and act on each part.
The signalperson whispers voice signals to keep the channel quiet, even when the operator struggles to hear them.
The signalperson shouts every word of a voice signal, because volume alone guarantees the message was understood.
The signalperson speaks as quickly as possible, because a faster signal always produces a faster and safer lift.

questions.explanation: A clear and steady pace lets the operator process function, direction, and distance in order instead of guessing at rushed words.

questions.question: A signaling crew is discussing main hoist versus auxiliary hoist for a signalperson. Which statement should guide the crew's work?

answers.text: For the signalperson, the auxiliary hoist is a backup drum that only turns when the main hoist drum fails during a lift.
For the signalperson, the whipline is a hand line the signalperson pulls to help the crane lift a load that feels too heavy.
For the signalperson, the main hoist handles the load block on the boom while the auxiliary hoist, often called the whipline, runs a lighter single line at the tip for quicker lighter picks.
For the signalperson, the main hoist and the auxiliary hoist are identical and either one can be signaled the same way on any pick.

questions.explanation: Knowing which hoist is rigged matters to the signalperson because the two lines move at different speeds and carry different kinds of picks.

questions.question: During a pre-lift review of agreeing on a backup plan if communication fails, which of the following should a signalperson affirm?

answers.text: Before the lift, the signalperson agrees with the operator on a backup plan for how movement will stop and communication will be restored if the chosen method fails.
Before the lift, the signalperson decides that if communication fails, the operator should finish the move from memory of the plan.
Before the lift, the signalperson leaves the failure response undecided so the crew can react flexibly in the moment.
Before the lift, the signalperson plans to keep signaling louder and faster if the chosen method starts to fail.

questions.explanation: A failure plan agreed in advance means a lost signal produces an immediate stop instead of guesswork while a load hangs in the air.

questions.question: During a pre-lift review of choosing emergency stop over stop during hoisting, which of the following should a signalperson affirm?

answers.text: When a hoisting movement must halt at once because of a sudden hazard, the signalperson gives the dog everything signal and points at the hazard.
When a hoisting movement must halt at once because of a sudden hazard, the signalperson drops both arms to the sides and steps backward.
When a hoisting movement must halt at once because of a sudden hazard, the signalperson gives the one-arm stop twice in rapid succession.
When a hoisting movement must halt at once because of a sudden hazard, the signalperson gives the two-arm emergency stop instead of the one-arm stop.

questions.explanation: The two-arm form marks urgency that the one-arm stop does not, so the signalperson reserves emergency stop for moments needing an immediate halt.

questions.question: Alex Morgan, a signalperson working at a commercial building site, is working on lowering on a tower crane by signal. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: On a tower crane, the signalperson uses the standard lower signal to lower the hook and load vertically toward a landing position.
On a tower crane, the signalperson uses the standard lower signal to stop all crane motion at the same time.
On a tower crane, the signalperson uses the standard lower signal to move the trolley outward along the jib away from the tower.
On a tower crane, the signalperson uses the standard lower signal to retract a telescoping boom section into the boom.

questions.explanation: Lower controls the vertical descent of the hook, so the signalperson keeps it distinct from trolley, swing, and stop commands.

questions.question: Nina Petrov, a signalperson working at a refinery turnaround site, is working on watching the boom tip as load comes on. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: As load first comes onto the crane, the signalperson watches the boom tip dip and shift to judge how much deflection is occurring before signaling the load any higher.
As load first comes on, the signalperson expects the tip to rise as weight is added, showing the boom is unloading.
As load first comes on, the signalperson closes the pick quickly because tip movement means the lift must be hurried.
As load first comes on, the signalperson watches only the load and never glances at the boom tip or its movement.

questions.explanation: The tip tells the story of the pick in real time. Its dip and shift show the signalperson how the boom is responding before the load leaves support.

questions.question: Marcus Webb, a signalperson working at a plant maintenance yard, is working on watching the boom and load approach toward power lines. Which of the following reflects sound practice?

answers.text: Watching the line is only necessary when the load itself is at its closest point, not while the boom is traveling toward it.
The signalperson should watch the load landing area and rely on the operator to notice any approach toward a line.
When work is near overhead lines, the signalperson watches the boom and load continuously as they approach the lines and warns the operator before clearance is threatened.
A warning about a power line should be given after the boom has entered the clearance zone so the operator knows it is serious.

questions.explanation: Clearance is lost gradually as the boom travels, so continuous watching and an early warning give the operator time to stop well before contact becomes possible.

nccco-service-truck-crane.quiz_title: Service Truck Crane Operator Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in setting up near an excavation edge?

answers.text: The truck should be positioned far enough from an excavation edge that soil failure or crumbling at the edge cannot undermine a stabilizer.
The truck can sit at an excavation edge whenever the trench walls look dry and have not crumbled yet that morning.
The truck is safe at an excavation edge if the stabilizer pad hangs partly over the edge to balance the truck weight.
The truck should be set as close to an excavation edge as possible so the boom reaches the work without repositioning.

questions.explanation: Soil near an open cut is already stressed and can shear away under added stabilizer pressure. Standing back from the edge keeps the support footprint on undisturbed ground that can carry the load reliably.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on interference from other transmitters?

answers.text: The operator continues lifting through interference as long as most commands still seem to work.
The operator raises transmitter power by holding it overhead when another remote interferes.
The operator commands motions twice quickly to push commands through any radio interference.
The operator stops and sorts out any interference or unexpected response before continuing, confirming the transmitter controls only the intended crane.

questions.explanation: Unexpected responses mean the control link cannot be trusted, so stopping to identify the interference and confirm the correct pairing protects against motion nobody commanded.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in winch and hook securing?

answers.text: Securing the hook is only needed when the truck will travel on a public highway afterward.
Loose load line may dangle from the tip overnight because its weight keeps it hanging straight.
At shutdown the operator reels in loose load line, secures the hook so it cannot swing freely, and leaves no loose rigging hanging from the boom tip.
The hook should be left hanging at head height so it is easy to grab at the next setup.

questions.explanation: A free-swinging hook or dangling line can strike a passerby, snag during travel, or damage the boom tip. Stowing line and hook neatly leaves the crane in the same controlled state expected at the next start.

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with safe practice in over rear working area?

answers.text: The over-the-rear working area is the area underneath the truck bed between the rear axles.
The over-the-rear working area is the sector directly over the cab where the boom is strongest.
The over-the-rear working area is any position where both stabilizers are fully retracted.
The over-the-rear working area is the sector behind the truck where the boom can work over the rear of the vehicle.

questions.explanation: Service truck cranes are described by working sectors around the truck, and the rear sector is defined by truck orientation rather than by stabilizer position or by the location of the cab.

questions.question: Which of the following is the soundest guidance on mental math for deductions?

answers.text: Because no calculator is provided, the operator should estimate deductions downward to save time.
Because no calculator is provided, the operator may skip small deductions to keep the math simple.
Because no calculator is provided for chart work, the operator should add deductions carefully in round steps and compare the total with the gross value before deciding the lift is allowed.
Because no calculator is provided, gross capacity alone may be used as the answer for any load.
