answers.text: The nursing assistant notes and reports how much of a meal the patient ate and any foods refused, because the nurse uses that observation to follow nutrition over time
The nursing assistant helps the patient to the toilet or offers the bedpan or urinal before meals when needed, because comfort needs met first make eating easier
After a meal, the nursing assistant helps the patient stay upright for a while when the care plan directs it, because remaining upright supports comfortable digestion
The nursing assistant helps the patient wash hands after toileting every time, because hand hygiene after the bathroom is a basic protection for the patient and others

questions.explanation: Comfort needs met first make eating easier and calmer. Toileting before meals is a simple part of good meal preparation.

questions.question: During post-mortem care for George, an 80-year-old patient in hospice care at home for advanced kidney disease, which infection-control practices still apply?

answers.text: The aide follows hand hygiene and standard precautions during care in the final days and during post-mortem care, just as with any other care
The aide continues routine comfort care in the final days even when the patient cannot respond, because comfort and dignity remain the goals of care
A patient near death may respond less to voices and touch, seeming distant or difficult to rouse even when family members speak nearby
If a dying patient seems restless when family steps out, the aide stays nearby, offers calm presence, and reports the restlessness to the nurse

questions.explanation: Hand hygiene and standard precautions apply in all care, including after death. They protect the aide, family, and others nearby.

questions.question: A daughter asks the aide to explain the care plan in detail. What is the aide's part in family teaching?

answers.text: The nursing assistant observes the patient during care and reports changes in condition to the registered nurse rather than interpreting them independently
The nursing assistant helps implement the team's plan during visits but never creates an independent plan of care for the patient or family
Teaching patients and families about their care plan is led by licensed team members, while the aide reinforces simple instructions as directed
The nursing assistant communicates with other team members through the registered nurse and team reports so information reaches the whole team

questions.explanation: Detailed teaching is led by licensed team members. The aide reinforces simple instructions only as the nurse directs.

questions.question: Virginia, an 80-year-old patient in palliative care in the hospital for advanced cancer, has slid down in the chair and is slumped. What is done?

answers.text: A patient who slides down in a chair is repositioned with help rather than left slumped, because slumping strains breathing and skin
A patient who cannot move independently is turned through a full range of comfortable positions across the day and night, not left on one side
After eating, a patient who has difficulty swallowing stays upright for a while as the care plan directs, and coughing or choking is reported
Walking with a patient begins with short distances and a planned place to sit and rest, building up only as the patient tolerates the activity

questions.explanation: A slumped posture cramps breathing and shears the skin. Repositioning with help restores both comfort and safe alignment.

questions.question: Raymond must stop in the middle of nearly every sentence to catch a breath and now speaks in short phrases. Which change is the nursing assistant seeing?

answers.text: Discomfort that appears mainly during movement or personal care and eases at rest is a pattern the nursing assistant describes to the RN, including when it happens
Crying, tearfulness, or calling out during care that was previously tolerated well is a change worth reporting to the RN as a possible sign of pain or distress
Needing to stop in the middle of a sentence to catch the breath, or speaking only in short phrases, is a breathing change the nursing assistant reports to the RN
A whistling sound heard when the patient breathes, which was not noticed before, is described factually to the RN by the nursing assistant

questions.explanation: Stopping mid-sentence for breath shows breathing is harder than before. That functional change is reported to the RN promptly.

questions.question: Rosa, an 85-year-old patient in an inpatient hospice unit for advanced cancer, is trying to nap while the hallway is busy. How can the nursing assistant make the room quieter for rest?

answers.text: The nursing assistant quiets the room for rest by lowering voices, softening light, and reducing unnecessary noise near a patient who is trying to sleep
The nursing assistant limits hallway noise and closes the door when the patient wishes, because ordinary facility sounds can keep a light sleeper awake for hours
The nursing assistant supports daytime activity and time out of bed as the care plan allows, because a balanced day usually leads to better rest at night
The nursing assistant dims lights and reduces stimulation in the evening to signal that night is coming, following the rhythm the patient finds restful

questions.explanation: Lowered voices, softer light, and less noise help a patient settle. Small changes near the room protect fragile rest.

questions.question: Helen, an 83-year-old patient in hospice care in an assisted living residence for advanced heart failure, grieves losses that have already happened during the illness. Which losses often weigh most heavily?

answers.text: Cultural and religious traditions shape mourning practices, rituals, and expectations, and the family's own practices guide how support is offered
Referring to the patient by name and listening to stories about them helps families feel their loved one is remembered as a person
Some families find comfort in viewing the body, washing rituals, prayer, or keepsakes after a death, and these wishes are respected within the plan of care
A patient's own grief may focus on losses already experienced, such as independence, familiar roles, privacy, and plans for the future

questions.explanation: Patients grieve losses already lived, not only the future. Independence, familiar roles, privacy, and plans all carry real weight.

questions.question: Samuel, a 76-year-old patient in hospice care at home for advanced neurologic disease, is weak and unsteady but asks to use the toilet. How should the nursing assistant handle safety while the patient is seated?

answers.text: During meals in a shared dining room, the nursing assistant seats patients comfortably, protects clothing as the patient wishes, and keeps the atmosphere calm and social
Water and drinks are refreshed during the day and stale or warm drinks are replaced, because fresh fluids within reach are more likely to be accepted by the patient
The nursing assistant stays nearby or within call reach while a weak patient uses the toilet and never leaves a patient who might fall sitting alone without support
The nursing assistant positions the call light within reach before leaving after toileting help so the patient can signal for assistance instead of getting up alone

questions.explanation: A weak patient is never left alone on the toilet unsupported. Staying nearby or within call reach prevents a fall.

chpn.quiz_title: CHPN (Certified Hospice and Palliative Nurse) Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Why are goals and decisions written into the plan of care?

answers.text: When goals conflict within a family, the patient's own stated wishes govern while the patient can express them
Symptom goals are stated measurably where possible — for example the pain level the patient finds acceptable — so the team can judge whether the plan is working
Reassessment is ongoing because hospice patients change quickly; each visit re-evaluates symptoms, function, and progress toward the stated goals
The nurse documents goals and decisions in the plan of care so every team member and covering clinician works from the same understanding

questions.explanation: Documentation aligns the whole team and covering clinicians on what the patient actually decided.

questions.question: During a painful procedure, which coaching helps the patient cope?

answers.text: Create a quiet, calm room and cluster care activities, because rest between disturbances protects comfort for a patient in pain
Offer repositioning, pillows for support, and alignment checks before assuming pain requires only medicine, because position is a common reversible cause
Teach family members simple hand massage and positioning, because involving loved ones gives them a concrete way to comfort the patient
Teach slow breathing and relaxation during painful procedures, because coached coping reduces distress while care is delivered

questions.explanation: Teaching slow breathing and relaxation during procedures reduces distress while care is delivered.

questions.question: Cultural and religious practices influence symptom care in which way?

answers.text: Cultural and religious practices around food, modesty, touch, and dying shape symptom care, so the nurse asks rather than assumes what a patient wants
Bleeding risk rises when platelets fall or the liver fails, so care avoids unnecessary invasive procedures and plans for calm management if bleeding occurs
Bone metastases weaken bone and raise fracture risk, so transfers and turning are done gently and new focal bone pain is reported promptly
Families often equate food with care, so declining intake near death needs gentle explanation that the body can no longer use nutrition as before

questions.explanation: Practices around food, modesty, touch, and dying shape acceptable care, so the nurse asks rather than assumes.

questions.question: What makes grief 'disenfranchised' for a mourner?

answers.text: Palliative sedation is the monitored lowering of consciousness for otherwise refractory suffering near death, undertaken with consent and team agreement
Withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatment are ethically equivalent when the treatment no longer serves the patient's goals; neither is required to continue
Post-mortem care prepares and positions the body respectfully, honours cultural and religious handling practices, and allows the family unhurried time before transfer
Disenfranchised grief is mourning that society does not openly recognize — such as for an ex-partner or a stigmatized death — leaving the griever unsupported

questions.explanation: The loss is not socially recognized or supported, so the griever mourns without the usual acknowledgment.

questions.question: Which presentation of options best supports an informed decision?

answers.text: Bring new assessment findings to the interdisciplinary group so the plan of care is revised by the whole team, not by one discipline alone
Frame treatment options by their benefits and burdens for this patient, because that framing is what makes a choice informed
Clarify who the patient's chosen decision maker is and record it, because confusion about authority surfaces at the worst moments
Reassess pain, symptoms, function, and caregiver strain at every visit, because change between visits is the rule in hospice care

questions.explanation: Options framed by what each gains and what each costs this patient, in plain language.

questions.question: A hospice patient suddenly worsens. What is assessed before calling it progression?

answers.text: As death nears over weeks, patients typically sleep more, eat less, withdraw socially, and need more help with every activity
Increasing symptom burden, repeated infections, and unplanned hospitalizations are progression signals across most life-limiting diseases
New or worsening symptoms in advanced disease are assessed for reversible causes first, because infection or medication effects can mimic progression
Frailty and dementia usually decline gradually over years, with dwindling function punctuated by minor illnesses that each take a lasting toll

questions.explanation: Reversible causes — infection, medication effects — are checked first because they can mimic progression.

questions.question: For persistent, continuous pain, why is scheduled around-the-clock dosing preferred?

answers.text: Physical dependence means withdrawal symptoms occur if an opioid is stopped abruptly, and it can occur in any patient taking opioids regularly
Respiratory depression is the most serious opioid adverse effect and is more likely with rapid increases, impaired clearance, or added sedatives
Around-the-clock scheduled analgesia is preferred for persistent pain because it maintains steadier relief than waiting for pain to return
Adjuvant analgesics are medicines developed for other purposes that also relieve specific pain types, such as neuropathic or bone pain

questions.explanation: Scheduled dosing maintains steadier relief for persistent pain than waiting for pain to return before treating.

questions.question: Urine stops draining through a catheter. What is checked before calling it bladder failure?

answers.text: Urinary retention can present as restlessness, agitation, or lower abdominal discomfort, especially in patients who cannot report symptoms clearly
Vomiting that persists despite treatment prompts review for obstruction, medicine effects, and raised pressure within the skull
A blocked or kinked urinary catheter is checked before retention is treated as new bladder failure, because mechanical causes are common and simple to fix
Skin care and scheduled toileting protect dignity and skin in incontinence, because prolonged moisture leads quickly to breakdown

questions.explanation: Tubing is checked for kinks and blockage first, because mechanical problems are common and simple to correct.

questions.question: After teaching a new care routine, how does the nurse confirm the caregiver understood?

answers.text: Document communication preferences — language, interpreter need, information style, and key contacts — so every team member communicates the way the patient chose
Summarize and check agreement at the end of family meetings, because participants often leave the same meeting with different understandings of what was decided
Explore spiritual concerns with open questions about meaning, hope, and sources of strength, and offer a chaplain visit without assuming religious identity
Use teach-back — asking the patient or caregiver to restate the plan in their own words — to confirm understanding without shaming the learner

questions.explanation: Teach-back: the caregiver restates the plan in her own words, revealing gaps without shame or testing.

questions.question: How should oxygen safety teaching be conducted in a particular household?

answers.text: Build a concrete respite plan with named helpers and scheduled breaks, because vague advice to 'take care of yourself' changes nothing
Demonstrate a care task first, then watch the caregiver perform it and correct gently, because guided practice builds real competence and confidence
Review oxygen safety in the actual home — flames, smoking, tubing routes — because generic warnings miss the hazards of a particular household
Stock and organize supplies with the caregiver and show where each item belongs, because a prepared home lowers panic when symptoms change

questions.explanation: In the home itself — checking flames, smoking habits, and tubing routes where the equipment actually sits.

questions.question: Ethel contrasts two quality approaches. Which one focuses on meeting set standards?

answers.text: Quality assurance focuses on meeting established standards and identifying deficiencies, while performance improvement proactively designs better processes
Patient and family satisfaction surveys are one data source among several and are interpreted alongside clinical outcome measures
Accurate, contemporaneous documentation is the legal and clinical record of care; late or altered entries undermine its credibility
Electronic health record audit trails track who accessed or changed a record and when, supporting accountability and privacy review

questions.explanation: Quality assurance focuses on meeting established standards and identifying deficiencies against them.

questions.question: During care of a nonverbal patient, which observations should the nurse watch for?

answers.text: Screen for depression, anxiety, and spiritual distress when pain seems out of proportion, because total pain amplifies physical symptoms
Observe for grimacing, guarding, bracing, restlessness, and altered breathing in a patient who cannot speak, because these behaviors signal pain
Validate the patient's report even when findings do not match expectations, because disbelieving reports damages trust and delays relief
Ask the patient to describe pain in their own words, including location and quality, because self-report guides all other assessment

questions.explanation: Grimacing, guarding, bracing, restlessness, and breathing changes are watched for in patients who cannot speak.

questions.question: Harold, a 79-year-old in the long-term care facility, develops a symptom crisis at home. Which mechanism adjusts the response?

answers.text: Hearing is commonly believed to persist late, so families are encouraged to keep talking to the patient even when there is no response
Changes in level of care, such as moving to continuous care during a symptom crisis, exist to match intensity of support to need
Death is pronounced after breathing and circulation have stopped and the patient is unresponsive; the nurse confirms and documents the time and findings
Terminal secretions — the 'death rattle' — come from pooled secretions the patient can no longer clear, and usually distress listeners more than the patient

questions.explanation: A change in level of care, such as continuous care, brings added nursing presence to the crisis.

questions.question: Noisy upper-airway breathing develops suddenly in a hospice patient. What does this sign require?

answers.text: Stridor and noisy upper-airway breathing signal airway narrowing and warrant prompt team assessment rather than routine reassurance
Gentle elevation and skin protection are central to edema care in hospice, because fragile edematous skin breaks down easily
Peripheral edema in advanced illness often reflects low protein, inactivity, organ failure, and medicines together rather than a single cause
Dyspnea is the patient's subjective sense of breathlessness, so the patient's own report guides assessment more than any single breathing measurement

questions.explanation: Stridor signals airway narrowing and needs prompt team assessment; it is never dismissed as a routine finding.

questions.question: An exhausted spouse needs a short break while the patient stays safe. Which level of care serves that purpose?

answers.text: Safe home medication practice includes secure storage away from children and visitors, an up-to-date medication list, and approved disposal of medications that are no longer used
Electing the Medicare hospice benefit means the patient chooses hospice care and gives up Medicare payment for curative treatment of the terminal illness, while unrelated coverage continues
A do-not-resuscitate order directs that cardiopulmonary resuscitation not be attempted if breathing or circulation stops; it does not by itself limit comfort care or other treatment
Hospice care is delivered at levels matched to need — routine home care, continuous home care, general inpatient care, and short inpatient respite care that relieves the caregiver

questions.explanation: Short inpatient respite care exists to relieve the caregiver while the patient's care continues safely.

questions.question: Eugene, an 84-year-old in the inpatient hospice unit, is being considered for admission. Which certification finding must be present?

answers.text: Hospice eligibility requires certification that the patient has a terminal illness with a life expectancy of six months or less if the illness runs its usual course
Routine home care is the most common level of hospice care, provided in the patient's residence with visits scheduled according to the plan of care
The hospice plan of care must be reviewed and updated by the interdisciplinary group at regular intervals and whenever the patient's condition changes
A hospice election statement documents that the patient chooses hospice care and understands that curative treatment for the terminal illness is waived under the benefit

questions.explanation: Admission requires the terminal prognosis certification; a serious diagnosis alone, without that prognosis, is not enough.

questions.question: Mildred, an 88-year-old in the inpatient hospice unit, with capacity refuses a recommended intervention. What principle governs?

answers.text: Practice guidelines support, but do not replace, clinical judgment tailored to the individual patient's goals and condition
Double effect describes an action intended to relieve suffering that may foreseeably hasten death, when relief, not death, is the intent
Allocation of scarce hospice resources is guided by need and fairness, not by ability to pay or social worth
Autonomy means a patient with decision-making capacity has the right to accept or refuse recommended care, even when the team disagrees with the choice

questions.explanation: The patient's autonomy governs; capacity, not team agreement, carries the right to refuse treatment.

questions.question: Arthur, an 80-year-old receiving home hospice care, has pain persisting long after an injury has healed, now affecting mood and daily function. Which description fits?

answers.text: Chronic or persistent pain continues beyond expected healing and may persist without ongoing tissue damage, affecting function and mood
Incident pain is a type of breakthrough pain triggered by a specific activity or movement such as walking, coughing, or wound care
A faces scale uses illustrated facial expressions to help children and patients with limited language or literacy report pain intensity
The location, onset, duration, character, aggravating and relieving factors, and effect on function together form a complete pain history

questions.explanation: Persistent pain outlasts healing, may continue without ongoing damage, and commonly impairs function and mood.

questions.question: During most seizures, what usually happens and what takes priority?

answers.text: Most seizures stop on their own within a short time, and the immediate priorities are protecting the patient from injury and keeping the airway clear
Common reversible contributors to delirium in hospice include infection, dehydration, constipation, urinary retention, and newly added or changed medications
Hyperactive delirium presents with restlessness, agitation, and heightened alertness, while hypoactive delirium presents with drowsiness, withdrawal, and quiet inattention
Status epilepticus is a prolonged or repeated seizure without a return to baseline between episodes and requires urgent team intervention

questions.explanation: Most seizures end on their own quickly; protecting the patient from injury and keeping the airway clear take priority.

questions.question: Joseph, a 78-year-old on the palliative care service, begins treating the nurse like a family friend. What framework guides the response?

answers.text: Professional boundaries protect the patient and family by keeping the relationship therapeutic, consistent, and focused on their needs, not the nurse's
Reflective practice, deliberately reviewing what happened and what was learned, turns experience into improved professional judgment
Debriefing with colleagues after a difficult death helps process grief and prevents unacknowledged loss from accumulating across patients
Maintaining licensure, competence, and required training is a personal professional responsibility, not solely the employer's

questions.explanation: Professional boundaries — the relationship stays therapeutic and focused on the patient and family needs.

rnc-mnn.quiz_title: RNC-MNN (Maternal Newborn Nursing) Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What does polyhydramnios in pregnancy signal for postpartum and newborn care?

answers.text: Postterm pregnancy increases risks for meconium passage, macrosomia, and placental insufficiency, with a newborn who may show dysmaturity features.
Polyhydramnios is associated with maternal diabetes and fetal anomalies and overdistends the uterus, increasing postpartum hemorrhage risk.
Preeclampsia can persist or first appear after birth, and postpartum eclampsia remains a risk during the early postpartum period.
Oligohydramnios is associated with fetal renal anomalies and prolonged membrane rupture and can contribute to pulmonary hypoplasia in the newborn.

questions.explanation: Excess fluid often points to diabetes or a fetal anomaly and leaves the uterus overstretched, raising hemorrhage risk.

questions.question: A wet newborn left uncovered loses heat mainly through which route?

answers.text: Newborns generate heat mainly through nonshivering thermogenesis, the metabolism of brown fat triggered by cold stress.
Fetal lung fluid is cleared during labor and the first breaths, largely by absorption into the pulmonary circulation and lymphatics.
The first breaths after birth inflate the lungs, establish functional residual capacity, and help the newborn maintain oxygenation.
Evaporation loses heat when moisture on the newborn's skin converts to vapor, especially just after birth while the skin is wet.

questions.explanation: Moisture evaporating from wet skin carries heat away quickly, which is why drying is one of the first steps after every birth.

questions.question: Warmth and oxygenation during recovery — what action should the nurse take?

answers.text: Massage the fundus gently until it feels firm when uterine atony is contributing to excessive bleeding.
Keep the patient warm, monitor oxygenation, and assess mental status while bleeding is being controlled.
Monitor for oozing from puncture sites, bruising, and bleeding gums that could signal a clotting disorder.
Teach the patient to report heavy bleeding, large clots, dizziness, or a feeling of faintness without delay.

questions.explanation: Understanding hemorrhage causes helps the nurse anticipate deterioration and act quickly to protect maternal safety.

questions.question: Infant size concerns in postpartum care — which statement is accurate?

answers.text: Infants of diabetic mothers may also be larger than average and at risk for birth related complications.
Breastfeeding can lower maternal glucose and may increase hypoglycemia awareness needs after delivery.
Infants of diabetic mothers are at risk for low blood sugar in the early hours after birth.
Patients with gestational diabetes often return to normal glucose levels after birth but remain at higher future risk.

questions.explanation: Communicating maternal diabetes at newborn handoff supports timely infant glucose monitoring in the early hours of life.

questions.question: Eye care during phototherapy requires the nurse to do what?

answers.text: Ensure bilirubin testing and follow-up are completed as ordered for newborns at higher risk or discharged early after birth
Shield the eyes of a newborn receiving phototherapy and check the shield position whenever providing care or feeding
Report jaundice appearing in the first day of life promptly, because early jaundice is treated as pathologic until evaluated
Monitor temperature, intake, output, and weight during phototherapy and report poor feeding or signs of dehydration promptly

questions.explanation: Eyes stay shielded during phototherapy, and shield position is checked at every care and feeding contact.

questions.question: What postpartum monitoring is essential for a patient who had fever during labor?

answers.text: Assess tone, respiratory effort, and alertness closely after birth in the newborn delivered after a Category III tracing and share cord gas results with the newborn team.
Monitor temperature and assess for uterine tenderness and foul-smelling lochia in the postpartum patient who had intrapartum fever.
Wait for the prescribed interval of delayed cord clamping in a vigorous term newborn while keeping the infant warm and assessing breathing.
Assess perineal trauma, fundal tone, and lochia carefully after an operative vaginal birth because lacerations increase bleeding and infection risk.

questions.explanation: Intrapartum infection can progress to endometritis, so fever, uterine pain, and lochia changes need continued review.

questions.question: Engorgement makes feeding uncomfortable for Amara. Which advice should the nurse give?

answers.text: Teach formula-feeding parents to hold the newborn semi-upright and pace bottle feedings with pauses.
Show the parent hand expression by gently compressing the breast tissue behind the areola with a rhythmic motion.
For engorgement, advise feeding frequently and applying cold compresses after feedings to reduce swelling and pain.
Demonstrate burping during and after feedings and teach parents to keep the newborn upright briefly after feeding.

questions.explanation: Frequent feeding drains the breast while cold after feedings eases swelling, making latch easier at the next session.

questions.question: Sexual activity after birth is raised by a patient. Which points should the nurse discuss?

answers.text: Discuss return to sexual activity in terms of comfort, healing, and contraception, noting that ovulation can occur before the first period.
Review perineal self-care at discharge, including hand hygiene, front-to-back cleansing, and pad changes to reduce infection risk.
Create a safety plan with a patient who discloses partner violence, including safe contacts, resources, and steps for leaving quickly.
Assess mood, sleep, support at home, and coping at each postpartum contact, and refer promptly when symptoms suggest depression.

questions.explanation: Ovulation can precede the first postpartum period, so contraception matters whenever sexual activity resumes after healing.

questions.question: Magnesium therapy monitoring during recovery — what action should the nurse take?

answers.text: Assess for calf pain and chest symptoms together when a breathless postpartum patient is evaluated.
Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, lung sounds, and urine output closely during magnesium therapy.
Elevate the head of the bed and give oxygen as directed when a patient develops acute breathlessness.
Report new crackles, frothy sputum, or falling oxygen saturation to the provider without delay.

questions.explanation: Careful monitoring during magnesium therapy helps detect toxicity early while supporting seizure prevention efforts.

questions.question: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis in postpartum care — which statement is accurate?

answers.text: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis involves infected clots in pelvic veins and can cause persistent fever despite treatment.
Fever appearing after the first day is more concerning for infection than a brief low grade rise immediately after birth.
Endometritis is infection of the uterine lining that typically presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and foul lochia.
Pyelonephritis in the postpartum period can cause flank pain, high fever, nausea, and vomiting.

questions.explanation: Maternal sepsis requires immediate recognition and escalation because delays increase the risk of organ dysfunction.

questions.question: Private screening setting following birth — which nursing action is appropriate?

answers.text: Monitor patients with bipolar disorder closely for decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and agitation.
Encourage rest, support at home, and help with infant care as part of recovery from postpartum depression.
Screen for intimate partner violence and substance use in a private, supportive setting when indicated.
Document screening results, safety assessment, referrals, and follow up plans clearly.

questions.explanation: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency, and continuous supervision with urgent psychiatric evaluation is the priority response.

questions.question: Examining the calves of a patient after cesarean birth, which practice is correct?

answers.text: Inspect the legs for redness, warmth, and swelling and ask about calf pain at each assessment.
Escalate promptly when the fundus remains boggy, bleeding increases, or vital signs show a concerning trend.
Document fundal height in relation to the umbilicus along with firmness and lochia findings.
Examine the perineum for redness, swelling, bruising, discharge, and approximation of any repair edges.

questions.explanation: Both legs are compared for size, warmth, and pain, because unilateral findings are the more concerning pattern.

questions.question: Pulse readings in the fifties in an asymptomatic patient on day two suggest which interpretation?

answers.text: Lochia alba is the whitish-yellow discharge that may continue for several weeks after birth.
Blood volume and cardiac output remain elevated immediately after birth and then gradually return toward prepregnancy levels.
A moderate amount of lochia that saturates a perineal pad over several hours without large clots can be expected early postpartum.
A slow pulse rate in the first week after birth is a common physiologic adaptation and is often called postpartum bradycardia.

questions.explanation: Postpartum bradycardia is a recognized adaptation, and it is interpreted alongside blood pressure and bleeding status.

questions.question: A vaginally born newborn's head looks elongated at birth, then rounds out. Which statement explains this?

answers.text: Epstein pearls are small white cysts along the newborn's gum line or palate that disappear without any treatment.
Molding is the temporary overlapping of the newborn's skull bones during passage through the birth canal that resolves after birth.
Vernix caseosa is the white, cheesy protective coating on the newborn's skin, more abundant in infants born earlier in gestation.
A newborn's resting heart rate and breathing rate are considerably faster than an older child's or an adult's normal rates.

questions.explanation: Molding lets the skull adapt to the birth canal, and the elongated shape normally rounds out within the first days after birth.

questions.question: At the moment of birth, which three questions form the rapid assessment that decides the first path of care?

answers.text: The rapid assessment at birth asks three questions: whether the baby is term, whether muscle tone is good, and whether the baby is breathing or crying.
A rising heart rate is the earliest and most reliable sign that ventilation of the newborn's lungs is effective.
Parents cope better during newborn resuscitation when a designated team member keeps them informed and a clear plan for updates and reunion is followed.
The Apgar score has five components: heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color, each scored from zero to two.

questions.explanation: Term status, tone, and breathing sort newborns in seconds. Babies who answer yes to all three stay with the mother; any no moves care to the warmer.

questions.question: During auscultation, an unexpected murmur is detected in a quiet newborn. Which interpretation is safest?

answers.text: Prematurity increases the risk of apnea and respiratory distress because lung maturity and breathing control are still developing
Central cyanosis involving the lips, tongue, and trunk is more concerning than blue hands and feet alone, which can be normal early after birth
A heart murmur in a newborn requires follow-up and context, because some murmurs are transitional while others signal structural heart disease
Chest movement that is uneven, with one side rising less, raises concern for an air leak or a lung problem on the less-moving side

questions.explanation: A murmur should never be dismissed without follow-up, since transitional sounds and structural disease can sound similar at first.

questions.question: Infection appearing in the first days after birth, linked to organisms acquired around delivery, is classified how?

answers.text: A newborn can be seriously infected while having a low or unstable temperature rather than a fever, especially in the first weeks
Early-onset sepsis appears in the first days after birth and is often linked to organisms acquired around the time of birth
Group B streptococcus is a well-recognized cause of early-onset newborn sepsis acquired around birth from maternal colonization
Late-onset sepsis develops after the first days of life and is more often linked to organisms acquired from the environment or caregivers

questions.explanation: Early-onset sepsis arises in the first days and is usually connected to organisms encountered around birth.

questions.question: Helping a patient void after birth, which measures are most appropriate?

answers.text: Encourage timed voiding, running water, and privacy to help the patient empty the bladder after birth.
Apply cold packs to the perineum intermittently during the first day to reduce swelling and discomfort.
Teach the patient to avoid prolonged sitting pressure and to use prescribed topical comfort measures for hemorrhoids.
Teach the patient to change perineal pads frequently and to inspect the pad for amount and odor each time.

questions.explanation: Timed attempts, privacy, and running water relax and cue voiding without resorting immediately to catheterization.

questions.question: On a cool evening, parents bundle their newborn in several heavy blankets for sleep. Which adjustment should the nurse suggest?

answers.text: Collect the metabolic screening sample after the first day of feeding and before discharge, and arrange a repeat screen when the first sample was drawn very early.
Teach the parents to dress the newborn in about one more layer than an adult would wear and to avoid overheating, which is a risk factor for unsafe sleep.
Teach the parents to keep the cord stump clean and dry, fold the diaper below it, and report spreading redness, drainage, foul odor, or bleeding from the stump.
Instruct the parents to seek care promptly for poor feeding, fever or unstable temperature, worsening jaundice, breathing difficulty, or signs of cord infection.

questions.explanation: Overheating is both a comfort and a safety issue for sleeping infants. About one extra layer, with the sleep surface kept bare, is the balanced guidance.

questions.question: Glucose assessment is a priority for which jittery newborn presentation?

answers.text: Arrange follow-up and early intervention referrals as directed for newborns with neurologic injury or congenital spinal defects
Inspect the perineum carefully after birth and report absence of an anal opening before feeding plans are assumed to be routine
Watch first feedings closely for coughing, choking, or color change and stop and report at once if those signs appear
Check blood glucose promptly in a jittery, poorly feeding newborn and follow the care plan for feeding or treatment without delay

questions.explanation: A jittery newborn who feeds poorly needs prompt glucose checking and timely follow-through on the care plan.

rnc-nic.quiz_title: RNC-NIC (Neonatal Intensive Care Nursing) Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What are the capabilities and limits of pulse oximetry in neonatal care?

answers.text: A rising lactate level signals that tissues are producing energy without enough oxygen, making lactate a useful marker of poor perfusion and worsening metabolic acidosis.
Surfactant replacement treats the surfactant deficiency of preterm respiratory distress syndrome by lowering surface tension, improving lung compliance and oxygenation.
Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxygen saturation noninvasively, but its readings are limited by motion, poor perfusion, and abnormal hemoglobin and do not measure ventilation.
High-flow nasal cannula delivers heated, humidified gas at flows that wash out upper airway dead space and provide a modest, variable distending pressure.

questions.explanation: Oximetry tracks oxygenation continuously but says nothing about carbon dioxide, so ventilation needs separate assessment.

questions.question: What is facilitated tucking, and what does it accomplish during a procedure?

answers.text: Facilitated tucking, in which a caregiver holds the infant limbs in a flexed contained position, reduces stress and pain responses during procedures.
A newborn can hear well at birth and turns toward familiar voices, while vision is best for objects held at close range in the early weeks.
Oral sucrose given with sucking for a brief painful procedure reduces behavioral pain responses in the neonate through a sweet-taste calming effect.
State and attentional stress cues in a neonate include gaze aversion, glassy-eyed staring, fussiness, and an inability to settle into sleep or alertness.

questions.explanation: Hands holding the infant flexed and contained mimic womb boundaries and lessen stress and pain responses.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes hemoglobin and hematocrit at birth?

answers.text: Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen more strongly than adult hemoglobin, and neonatal red cells live a shorter time than adult red cells before breaking down.
Neonatal hemoglobin and hematocrit are normally higher than adult values at birth and fall over the first weeks as fetal red cells are replaced.
Polycythemia raises blood viscosity, and hyperviscosity can impair flow to the brain, gut, kidneys, and lungs in the affected newborn.
Hemolytic disease raises indirect bilirubin because red cells are destroyed faster than the immature liver can conjugate the bilirubin load.

questions.explanation: Newborn values start high because of fetal red cell mass, then fall as those cells age and production slows.

questions.question: How should a new genetic diagnosis be communicated to parents?

answers.text: Connect parents with condition-specific family support organizations and early intervention referral after a genetic diagnosis is confirmed.
Communicate a new genetic diagnosis in a private setting, using plain language, allowing silence, and checking what the parents have understood.
Support parents in telling extended family about a heritable condition because relatives may share risk and benefit from their own evaluation.
Coordinate confirmatory chromosome or molecular testing and ensure results are communicated to the family with counseling support available.

questions.explanation: Privacy, plain words, and time to absorb the news help parents hear difficult information without added confusion.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of structured developmental follow-up after NICU discharge?

answers.text: Corrected age, calculated from the due date, is used when interpreting growth and developmental milestones for a preterm infant during the first years of life.
A car seat challenge screens a preterm or low-birth-weight infant for apnea, bradycardia, and oxygen desaturation while positioned in the car seat before discharge.
Developmental follow-up after NICU discharge monitors motor, cognitive, and language milestones because preterm infants carry increased risk for delay and cerebral palsy.
Back-to-sleep positioning for every sleep, on a firm flat surface without soft bedding, lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome after discharge.

questions.explanation: Serial milestone checks catch motor, cognitive, and language delay early, when intervention helps development most.

questions.question: Why can birth weight alone not be used to decide how mature a newborn is at delivery?

answers.text: Birth weight alone does not establish maturity, because a growth-restricted term infant can weigh less than a normally grown preterm infant.
Intrauterine growth restriction describes a fetus that failed to reach its growth potential, often from placental insufficiency, and may be symmetric or asymmetric.
The Ballard examination estimates gestational age from physical signs and neuromuscular signs such as posture, arm recoil, and the scarf sign.
In asymmetric growth restriction, head growth is relatively spared while weight lags, reflecting late placental insufficiency with brain-sparing blood flow.

questions.explanation: Weight reflects growth as well as maturity, so dating and examination must be combined before risks are assigned to an infant.

questions.question: How should the nurse care for the central line delivering parenteral nutrition?

answers.text: Use strict aseptic technique for central line care and tubing changes for parenteral nutrition, and report fever, redness, or line leakage immediately.
Monitor ostomy output, stool losses, hydration, and electrolytes closely in the infant with short gut, and advance feedings only as tolerance allows.
Advance postoperative feedings gradually after repair of a gastrointestinal anomaly, watching the abdomen, output, and comfort with each increase.
Mix ordered energy supplements into feedings carefully, label the prepared feeding clearly, and reassess tolerance and growth after the change.

questions.explanation: Meticulous aseptic line care is the main defense against bloodstream infection in an infant receiving intravenous nutrition.

questions.question: Which infant is best cared for on a radiant warmer rather than in an incubator?

answers.text: Observe a cold infant closely for rising oxygen need, apnea, and worsening respiratory distress and escalate care as needed.
Monitor axillary temperature frequently during admission and rewarming and adjust support in response to the trend.
Rewarm a cold infant gradually while monitoring oxygen needs, glucose, and acid-base status throughout the process.
Use a radiant warmer for an unstable infant who needs frequent access, close observation, and repeated procedures.

questions.explanation: An unstable infant needing constant access and procedures benefits from the open bed despite its greater heat and water losses.

questions.question: How can infectious colitis be distinguished from allergic colitis clinically?

answers.text: Duodenal atresia blocks the duodenum, producing early bilious emesis, a double-bubble pattern on imaging, and an association with Down syndrome.
Imperforate anus ranges from a low membrane to a high malformation with fistula and requires evaluation for associated vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies.
Infectious colitis tends to make an infant systemically ill with fever and diarrhea, while allergic colitis often affects a well-appearing infant with bloody stools.
The preterm gastrointestinal tract shows immature motility, weak sphincter tone, limited digestive enzyme activity, and a permeable mucosal barrier.

questions.explanation: Systemic illness favors infection, while a well infant with bloody stools more often has an allergic cause.

questions.question: How can the nurse best support parents whose newborn has ambiguous genitalia?

answers.text: Support the family of the infant with ambiguous genitalia by using the name they choose, avoiding assumptions, and coordinating consistent information from the team.
Measure and record all urine output strictly, weigh diapers, and trend output over time rather than judging from a single wet diaper.
Position and handle the infant with bladder exstrophy to keep the exposed bladder moist and protected and to avoid traction on any drainage tubing.
Assess for bladder distention, a poor urinary stream, and catheter patency in the infant with suspected obstructive uropathy, and report retention promptly.

questions.explanation: Consistent information, chosen names, and freedom from assumptions help parents cope while evaluation proceeds.

questions.question: What does congenital adrenal hyperplasia screening aim to detect before crisis?

answers.text: Phenylketonuria screening depends on the infant having received protein feeding, so a specimen collected before adequate feeding may need to be repeated.
Early hypocalcemia occurs in the first days of life and is associated with prematurity, birth stress, and maternal diabetes.
Low serum calcium in the newborn is interpreted together with albumin, pH, and clinical signs, because total calcium alone can misrepresent the active ionized fraction.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia screening detects the classic salt-wasting form, in which cortisol and aldosterone deficiency can progress to shock.

questions.explanation: Salt-wasting disease can collapse quickly once sodium and fluid losses mount, so presymptomatic detection is protective.

questions.question: What communication completes the resuscitation nurse's responsibilities at handoff?

answers.text: Assign Apgar scores at the standard intervals after birth without interrupting or delaying any resuscitation that the newborn needs.
Call for additional help early, state role assignments clearly, and use closed-loop communication throughout the resuscitation.
Communicate the resuscitation events, interventions, and the newborn's responses clearly to the receiving team and document them in sequence.
Give epinephrine through vascular access as the preferred route when the heart rate stays low despite effective ventilation and coordinated compressions.

questions.explanation: A clear sequential account of events and responses lets the receiving team continue care without repeating steps.

questions.question: Which newborn findings are most characteristic of congenital cytomegalovirus infection acquired before birth?

answers.text: Cesarean birth without labor increases the newborn's risk for transient tachypnea because lung fluid is cleared more slowly than after vaginal birth.
Breech and other malpresentations increase the newborn's risk for birth trauma, developmental dysplasia of the hip, and cord prolapse during delivery.
Systemic opioid analgesia given close to delivery can cause respiratory depression and sedation in the newborn after birth.
Congenital cytomegalovirus infection can cause growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, hearing loss, and petechiae in the newborn.

questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus crosses the placenta and injures the developing brain, ears, and blood-forming tissues of the fetus.

questions.question: During the eye examination, the red reflex is absent in one eye of a newborn. What is the best nursing action?

answers.text: Inspect and palpate the abdomen and note distension, bowel sounds, cord vessels, and any mass before feeding the critically ill newborn.
Evaluate any vesicular, bullous, or pustular skin lesion in the critically ill newborn for infection rather than assuming a benign rash.
Assess color, tone, cry, and state first by observation before handling the newborn, because handling changes behavior and vital signs.
Check the red reflex in both eyes and refer promptly when the reflex is absent, dull, or asymmetric in the newborn.

questions.explanation: The red reflex is quick to check at the bedside, and an abnormal result needs specialist review rather than repeat watching.

questions.question: What mechanism underlies transient tachypnea of the newborn, and how does it typically evolve?

answers.text: Transient tachypnea of the newborn results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid and typically causes tachypnea that resolves within the first day or two after birth.
Apnea of prematurity is a developmental pause in breathing with bradycardia or desaturation that reflects immature respiratory control in the preterm infant.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia allows abdominal contents into the chest, compressing the developing lung and causing pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.
Respiratory distress syndrome results from surfactant deficiency in the preterm lung and presents with grunting, retractions, nasal flaring, and a ground-glass pattern on imaging.

questions.explanation: Retained lung fluid clears over hours to a couple of days, so tachypnea improves steadily without surfactant treatment.

questions.question: Why is the trend of head circumference more informative than one measurement in suspected hydrocephalus?

answers.text: A head circumference that crosses percentiles upward over time is more concerning for hydrocephalus than any single large measurement alone.
Neonatal seizures are often subtle, showing as eye deviation, lip smacking, bicycling movements, apnea, or autonomic changes rather than clear convulsions.
Germinal matrix vessels in preterm infants are fragile and vulnerable to swings in blood flow, blood pressure, and carbon dioxide in the first days of life.
Facial nerve injury after birth causes weakness on one side of the face, most visible when the infant cries, with incomplete eye closure on that side.

questions.explanation: A single large head may be familial, but a curve crossing upward shows fluid accumulating faster than growth.

questions.question: A newborn is cyanotic at rest but pinks up when crying. Which condition explains this pattern?

answers.text: Subgaleal hemorrhage bleeds into a large potential space beneath the scalp aponeurosis and can cause hypovolemia and shock, especially after vacuum-assisted birth.
Bilateral choanal atresia causes cyanosis at rest that improves with crying, because the newborn breathes preferentially through the nose and crying opens the mouth airway.
A cephalhematoma increases the newborn's risk for hyperbilirubinemia because the collected blood breaks down as the swelling resolves.
Micrognathia in Pierre Robin sequence lets the tongue fall backward and obstruct the airway, so positioning strongly influences breathing in these infants.

questions.explanation: Crying forces mouth breathing around blocked nasal passages, which is the classic clue to choanal atresia.

questions.question: Ruby, a term infant admitted on day of life 2 with jaundice in the intensive care nursery, Insensible losses are high on an open warmer. What environmental change reduces them?

answers.text: Maintain strict intake and output records that include parenteral fluids, feeds, urine, stool, and gastric losses for every shift.
Use a humidified incubator rather than an open warmer when feasible for a very preterm newborn whose insensible losses are high.
Review serum electrolyte results on schedule and compare each value with prior results to spot trends before symptoms appear.
Verify catheter placement and patency and confirm the prescribed solution and infusion device settings before starting parenteral fluids.

questions.explanation: Enclosed humidified air cuts evaporation from immature skin far better than an open warmer environment can.

questions.question: An infant who received prolonged opioid therapy in the unit becomes irritable as therapy is weaned. What explains this?

answers.text: An infant treated for a prolonged period with opioids or sedatives can develop physical dependence and show withdrawal when therapy is reduced or stopped.
Immature renal function and low glomerular filtration in the neonate slow drug excretion, prolonging the effect of medications cleared by the kidneys.
Intramuscular absorption in the neonate is erratic because muscle mass is small and peripheral perfusion varies with illness and temperature.
Topical absorption through neonatal skin is increased, especially in preterm infants, because the skin is thin and the surface area relative to weight is large.

questions.explanation: Dependence can develop from treatment itself, not only from maternal use, and withdrawal follows a too-rapid reduction.

questions.question: An outbreak of the same organism is identified among several nursery infants. What infection control action is appropriate?

answers.text: Inspect skin, cord, and line sites daily for pustules, redness, or discharge that may signal staphylococcal infection in the hospitalized neonate.
Monitor temperature, perfusion, feeding tolerance, and respiratory status closely and escalate promptly when a preterm infant shows subtle changes from baseline.
Begin empiric therapy directed at the most likely early-onset organisms once cultures are obtained, then narrow or stop therapy as culture results return.
Cohort infants with the same confirmed infection and use dedicated equipment when an outbreak or resistant organism is identified in the nursery.

questions.explanation: Grouping infected infants and dedicating equipment contain spread while the source and transmission route are investigated.

capa.quiz_title: CAPA (Certified Ambulatory Perianesthesia Nurse) Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: Which description fits general anesthesia as used in an ambulatory center?

answers.text: Epidural anesthesia in ambulatory practice delivers medication outside the spinal fluid space, often through a fine catheter, giving segmental numbness that can be prolonged for ongoing pain control

A spinal anesthetic for a same-day procedure places medication inside the spinal fluid space, so numbness and weakness develop quickly below the waist and then recede in a predictable pattern during Phase II

Day-of-surgery suitability for general anesthesia in a freestanding center depends on airway history, fasting compliance, stability of chronic conditions, and availability of a responsible adult at home

In an ambulatory center, general anesthesia is chosen when a procedure needs complete unawareness along with control of movement and pain, with breathing supported until the patient can protect the airway again

questions.explanation: Ambulatory general anesthesia is selected when complete unawareness plus control of movement and pain are needed, with breathing supported until airway protection returns.

questions.question: What completes a warming intervention before an ambulatory patient is discharged?

answers.text: Before discharge after throat surgery, teach the patient and escort that any fresh bleeding from the mouth at home is reported urgently, even if it seems small or stops on its own

At pre-anesthesia review, ask a patient with diabetes about early fullness, reflux, and vomiting of undigested food, and pass those answers to the anesthesia team as possible signs of delayed stomach emptying
Give nasal surgery discharge teaching that distinguishes light oozing from steady bright bleeding, and instruct the patient to avoid nose blowing and straining during early healing at home
Measure temperature during Phase II recovery, apply warming as ordered for a patient who is cold and shivering, and recheck temperature and comfort before discharge is finalized

questions.explanation: A recheck of temperature and comfort completes warming; discharge is not finalized on the basis of a blanket alone.

questions.question: Before anything is infused in Phase II, what is checked at the line site?

answers.text: Position changes in Phase II are done on a planned basis with bony areas padded, because a still-sedated patient cannot shift weight or report pressure discomfort
New confusion in extended care is reported with the patient's recent electrolyte results and intake history, because mental change can be an early sign of imbalance
At each Phase II check, intravenous line sites are looked at for swelling, leaking, redness, or pain before fluids or medicines are given through them
When a Phase II patient is moved, the head, neck, and limbs are kept in supported, neutral alignment to avoid stretch or pressure injury to nerves and joints

questions.explanation: Swelling, leaking, redness, or pain at the site are checked first, because fluids and medicines should not run through a compromised line.

questions.question: Why are family and the escort included in teaching when the patient agrees?

answers.text: Including family and the escort in teaching, with the patient's agreement, prepares the people who will handle medicines, wound checks, meals, mobility help, and observation at home
Teaching about the escort and transport role is part of discharge education, because the responsible adult must know how to help, what to watch for, and when to seek help after leaving
Discharge teaching in ambulatory care is delivered both by spoken review and in written form, because the written copy is what the patient and family consult during the first days at home
Education has worked when the patient or escort can describe and, for hands-on care, show what to do at home — handing over papers without that confirmation does not prove learning

questions.explanation: They will handle medicines, wound checks, meals, mobility help, and observation once the patient is home.

questions.question: What is reviewed during a post-discharge follow-up call?

answers.text: Discharge home from Phase II is appropriate only when the patient meets recovery criteria for alertness, circulation, breathing, movement, pain and nausea control, and surgical site condition
A post-discharge follow-up call reviews pain control, nausea, wound condition, medicines, activity, and new concerns, and gives the patient a chance to ask questions after the first period at home

Pre-admission phone screening for ambulatory surgery collects health history, allergies, current medicines and supplements, prior anesthesia experiences, and home support so risks are known before the day of surgery

Each transfer along the ambulatory continuum — pre-admission to day-of care, day-of care to recovery, and recovery to home — requires current information to travel with the patient so nothing is assumed or repeated unnecessarily

questions.explanation: Pain, nausea, wound condition, medicines, activity, and new concerns are reviewed once the patient has spent time at home.

questions.question: A patient asks why an opioid can make breathing slow at home. Which explanation is correct?

answers.text: Propofol given through the vein produces sleep for induction and upkeep of anesthesia, yet it offers no pain relief on its own, so separate comfort measures remain necessary
Opioid pain medicines ease surgical pain and soften stress responses, but in Phase II and at home they can slow breathing, cause sleepiness, nausea, itching, and constipation
Naloxone blocks opioid effects and can restore breathing when opioids have slowed it too much, but breathing can slow again if the opioid remains active longer than the blocker
Medicines such as ondansetron lessen nausea and vomiting after ambulatory surgery by interrupting signals along the pathways that trigger the vomiting reflex

questions.explanation: Opioids soften stress responses and ease pain, but they can also slow breathing and cause sleepiness, nausea, itching, and constipation during home recovery.

questions.question: Which discharge step is completed for a patient after spinal anesthesia who has not yet passed urine?

answers.text: For a patient with diabetes, follow the day-of-surgery glucose plan agreed in advance, check glucose in Phase II when behavior or alertness changes, and report a result outside the agreed plan promptly
Confirm at discharge that walking aids, glasses, and hearing aids used at baseline are returned and working, because safe mobility and communication at home depend on those familiar supports
When a laboratory result shows a sodium or potassium problem, keep the patient in monitored Phase II care, review the result with the anesthesia team, and hold discharge until a plan is in place

Before discharge after spinal anesthesia or pelvic surgery, assess for bladder fullness, assist a voiding attempt with privacy and upright positioning, and escalate a bladder that stays full and cannot empty

questions.explanation: Assessment for a full bladder and an assisted voiding attempt precede discharge, with escalation if the bladder cannot empty.

questions.question: What combination of findings defines readiness for Kevin, a 29-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing tonsillectomy, to be discharged home from Phase II?

answers.text: Successful voiding before discharge is required after certain procedures, anesthesia types, and for patients at higher risk of urinary retention per facility policy
Before discharge home, the ambulatory patient must have a responsible adult escort and a plan for adult companionship during the first period at home
Discharge readiness in Phase II is a combined judgment of stable vital signs, controlled pain and nausea, safe walking, and ability to take fluids as required by policy
A Phase II patient who still needs frequent intervention for pain, nausea, bleeding, or breathing support is not ready for discharge even if considerable time has passed

questions.explanation: Readiness combines stable vital signs, controlled pain and nausea, safe walking, and ability to take fluids as required by policy.

questions.question: Recovery in Phase II is slow and discharge today looks unsafe for Mark. What should the nurse recommend?

answers.text: Record every handoff, teaching session, discharge decision, and follow-up contact so the ambulatory record shows a continuous chain from pre-admission through home
Coordinate the ambulatory plan with anesthesia, the procedural team, Phase II colleagues, and family so pre-admission findings actually shape day-of and discharge decisions
Recommend extended care observation when Phase II recovery is progressing too slowly for safe discharge home, and explain the extended stay and its purpose to the patient and family

When the patient moves from Phase I into Phase II, give a concise structured report on procedure, anesthesia, block, stability, symptoms, and watch items, and confirm the Phase II nurse is ready to receive

questions.explanation: Extended care observation, explained clearly to the patient and family as continued monitoring rather than failure.

questions.question: Carol, a 51-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing endoscopic sinus surgery, is recovering in Phase II. Why do noise and crowding matter?

answers.text: Language, hearing, vision, and health literacy differences require adapted communication in ambulatory care, because standard rapid instructions fail patients who cannot fully receive them
Noise, bright light, and crowded activity in Phase II and extended care can heighten anxiety and disturb rest, so a calmer surroundings plan is part of individualized ambulatory recovery
Habits involving alcohol, tobacco, and other substances affect anesthesia recovery, nausea, pain control, and wound healing, and they are explored respectfully as part of ambulatory assessment
Anxiety and depression influence how pain is experienced, how teaching is absorbed, and how confidently a patient manages recovery at home, so they are considered in every ambulatory plan

questions.explanation: Noise, light, and activity can heighten anxiety and disturb rest, so calmer surroundings are part of individualized recovery.

questions.question: Why does Phase II observation continue even after a moderate sedation procedure is finished?

answers.text: For extended-care observation after total intravenous anesthesia, continue pulse oximetry and frequent alertness checks until the patient is consistently awake, breathing comfortably, and tolerating oral fluids
If a Phase II patient after general anesthesia for laparoscopy still feels unsteady, delay ambulation, reassess alertness and vital signs, and keep a staff member within reach during the first walk

For a patient recovering in Phase II after moderate sedation for colonoscopy, keep observation going until alertness returns to baseline, because drowsiness can linger after stimulation from the procedure ends

Before discharge home after spinal anesthesia for hernia repair, verify that leg strength and feeling have returned, the patient can walk safely, and voiding has occurred or a clear bladder plan is in place

questions.explanation: Phase II observation continues because drowsiness can linger after stimulation ends, and discharge waits until alertness has returned to the patient baseline.

questions.question: What does pre-admission teaching cover for Michelle, a 36-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing hysteroscopy, before ambulatory surgery?

answers.text: Pre-admission teaching for ambulatory surgery covers arrival time, fasting, medicines to take or hold as instructed, what to bring, escort requirements, and what recovery at home will involve
Teaching about the escort and transport role is part of discharge education, because the responsible adult must know how to help, what to watch for, and when to seek help after leaving

Day-of-surgery teaching in the ambulatory center reinforces pre-admission instructions, corrects misunderstandings, and prepares the patient and family for the procedure and the recovery sequence ahead
Sound communication for ambulatory teaching uses plain words, small amounts of information at a time, time for questions, and checks for understanding spread through the conversation

questions.explanation: Arrival, fasting, medicines, belongings, escort requirements, and home recovery are all covered before the surgery day.

questions.question: Linda, a 48-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing laparoscopic tubal ligation, is an infant whose temperature is drifting down in Phase II. What should the nurse do?

answers.text: Ask about alcohol and substance use during pre-anesthesia review in a nonjudgmental way and watch Phase II for early withdrawal signs so the team can respond early
Measure temperature and use active warming for infants and children in Phase II, since their small size lets body heat fall quickly during and after a procedure
Stay with a thrashing, inconsolable child in Phase II, protect against falls and line pulling, check for pain and low oxygen, and keep the environment calm until the episode settles
Bring a parent or trusted caregiver to the bedside early in a child's Phase II recovery when the unit allows, because a familiar voice helps calm fear and helps staff tell pain apart from fright

questions.explanation: Temperature is measured and active warming is used for infants and children in Phase II because small size lets body heat fall quickly during and after procedures.

questions.question: Nausea returns during the ride home and Betty, a 66-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing dilation and curettage, is still drowsy. How should the family position the patient?

answers.text: Written discharge materials reinforce breathing warning signs in plain language so the patient and family can recognize problems after leaving the center
Families are taught to position a still-drowsy patient on the side during the ride home and at home if nausea returns, while keeping the airway observable
Discharge teaching covers keeping follow-up contact information available and calling promptly for increasing breathlessness, wheezing, or fever with cough after surgery
Patients are advised not to drive, make important decisions, or be left alone while drowsy from lingering anesthetic and pain medicines after discharge home

questions.explanation: A still-drowsy patient is positioned on the side if nausea returns, keeping the airway observable during the ride home and at home.

questions.question: Thomas, a 34-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing septoplasty, reports ringing ears and a metallic taste shortly after a regional block. How are these reports treated?

answers.text: A severe allergic reaction in the ambulatory unit can follow a medicine, latex, or a blood product and combines hives or swelling with wheeze and falling blood pressure
A falling oxygen level in Phase II is a sign to work through airway, breathing, and circulation causes in order, because the number alone does not name the problem
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity can follow a regional block and may begin with ringing ears, a metallic taste, or agitation before progressing to seizures or heart effects
Laryngospasm in a patient waking after a same-day procedure is a sudden closing of the vocal cords that blocks air movement and can follow airway irritation or secretions

questions.explanation: As possible early signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity, which can progress to seizures or heart effects if the warning is missed.

questions.question: Charles, a 50-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy, develops muscle rigidity and a rapidly climbing temperature in Phase II. What should the nurse do?

answers.text: Call the discharged patient at the planned follow-up time, ask about pain, nausea, bleeding, and understanding of instructions, and escalate concerns to the surgical team
Share the center's outcome data at the quality meeting, help pilot the agreed change on a small scale, and compare new results with the baseline
If rigidity and a rapidly climbing temperature appear in Phase II, treat malignant hyperthermia as the working concern, stop likely triggers, and ready the crisis cart and dantrolene
When a child in extended care worsens, shift to pediatric-sized equipment and weight-based thinking and summon clinicians with pediatric expertise promptly

questions.explanation: Rigidity with a fast-climbing temperature in Phase II is treated as malignant hyperthermia until disproven, with triggers stopped and the cart readied.

questions.question: Carol, a 51-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing endoscopic sinus surgery, asks for a quieter corner of the recovery area to rest. What should the nurse do?

answers.text: Notice rising anxiety or low mood during Phase II, respond with calm orientation and unhurried presence, and involve family or additional support when distress continues
Match explanations and choices to developmental level, using play and parental presence for a child, direct involvement for an adolescent, and full partnership for an adult
Reduce avoidable noise and activity around a restless or anxious patient in Phase II, move non-urgent conversation away from the bedside, and dim harsh light when the setting allows
Ask what faith, cultural, or personal practices the patient wants honored during the visit, and arrange family presence, dietary respect, or spiritual support accordingly

questions.explanation: Honor the request where feasible by reducing surrounding noise and activity, treating calm surroundings as care.

questions.question: Why does the ambulatory nurse record how Margaret, a 67-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing cataract extraction with intraocular lens implant, normally breathes and exercises at the pre-anesthesia visit?

answers.text: A baseline symptom review in pre-anesthesia care matters because stable, longstanding findings can then be distinguished from new chest pain or a rhythm change arising later in Phase II

Heart failure that is decompensated on the day of surgery, shown by new breathlessness at rest, trouble breathing lying flat, and worsening swelling, makes elective ambulatory care unsuitable until the condition is evaluated and stabilized

Raised blood pressure discovered at day-of-surgery check-in is not judged as an isolated reading; accompanying symptoms, usual medicines, and anesthesia input together determine whether an elective ambulatory case proceeds

A pre-anesthesia baseline that records usual breathing effort, home oxygen use, and exercise tolerance gives the Phase II team a personal reference for judging whether recovery breathing has returned to the patient's normal

questions.explanation: A personal baseline prevents normal-for-this-patient findings from being misread in Phase II and makes real change visible.

questions.question: When is extra caution needed before Linda, a 48-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing laparoscopic tubal ligation, receives a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicine after a day procedure?

answers.text: Nausea and vomiting after a day procedure are more likely when there is a history of motion sickness, earlier postoperative nausea, or a need for opioid pain medicine
Long-standing daily pain treatment before surgery can change what a patient needs afterward, because tolerance and regular home medicines shape the discharge plan
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines ease pain and inflammation and are reviewed carefully when there is stomach, kidney, bleeding, or certain heart history
A pain score is most useful when the same descriptive approach is used each time and the patient's own words about location and character are recorded with it

questions.explanation: Stomach, kidney, bleeding, or certain heart histories call for careful review, because this drug group can aggravate each of those problems.

questions.question: A nurse realizes discharge paperwork for Amanda, a 47-year-old same-day surgery patient undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy, was sent to the wrong recipient. What is the correct next step?

answers.text: Escalate a misdirected message or other suspected disclosure through the center's privacy reporting route the same day, without attempting to hide or quietly undo it
Before discharge teaching begins, confirm the patient's chosen escort and the patient's permission for that person to hear medication and wound-care instructions
If family press for details a patient has asked to keep private, explain the limit courteously, offer to help the patient share what they choose, and inform the charge nurse
During the pre-admission call, ask whether an advance directive exists, note the response in the record, and invite the patient to bring a copy on the day of surgery

questions.explanation: A suspected disclosure is escalated through the center's privacy reporting route the same day; hiding it or quietly undoing it compounds the breach.

cpan.quiz_title: CPAN (Certified Post Anesthesia Nurse) Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam

questions.question: What is emergence in anesthesia recovery?

answers.text: General anesthesia produces reversible unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, and muscle relaxation, with airway and ventilation often supported by the anesthesia team
Dissociative sedation separates perception from surroundings while airway reflexes and spontaneous breathing are often better preserved than in deep sedation
Emergence is the return from general anesthesia toward wakefulness, when airway reflexes and consciousness recover and extubation readiness is judged
Epidural anesthesia places local anesthetic or analgesic in the epidural space, allowing a catheter for continued effect and a block that can be adjusted over time

questions.explanation: Emergence is the return toward wakefulness as reflexes and consciousness recover and extubation readiness is judged.

questions.question: How is the abdomen of George followed after abdominal surgery?

answers.text: After throat surgery, watch for frequent swallowing, restlessness, and blood in the mouth, and report these bleeding clues without waiting for visible hemorrhage
Inspect dressings and the wound area at arrival and repeatedly, marking and reporting expanding drainage or bleeding rather than simply reinforcing and forgetting the dressing
Assess the abdomen for distension, bowel sounds, nausea, and passage of gas, and report worsening distension or bloody output promptly
Report fever accompanied by wound changes, breathlessness, or falling blood pressure promptly, because the company a fever keeps determines its urgency
